CP-Agent: A Calibrated Risk-Controlled Agent for Feedback-Driven Competitive Programming

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: Make sure to enter the correct conference title from your rights confirmation email; June 03–05, 2018; Woodstock, NYISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2018/06CCS: Computing methodologies Natural language processingCCS: Mathematics of computing Stochastic processes
Peisong Wang Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China , Bowen Liu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China , Zehua Li Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China , Yuyao Wang Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China , Zhiwei Ma Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China , Yuhan Li Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China and Jia Li Note: Corresponding author. 2026
Abstract.

Large language models still struggle with contest-level programming, while many agentic remedies rely on massive inference-time sampling or expensive multi-stage post-training. We study when execution feedback reliably helps an LLM CP solver and which mechanisms govern the gains. We model feedback-driven solving as a calibrated stopped process and identify three quantities: false-admission risk, program-level evidence against bad programs, and the active-state success hazard. Under held-out trace calibration and selection from a pre-declared finite controller manifest, the resulting structural certificate lower-bounds the clean success probability before false admission. We instantiate mechanisms targeting these quantities as Dual-Granularity Verification, Test Augmentation, and Experience-Driven Self-Evolving, yielding CP-Agent. Without updating any parameters, CP-Agent raises Pass@1 from 25.8% to 48.5% on LiveCodeBench Pro and improves Refine@5 by 11.0% on ICPC-Eval. Across three LLM backbones, CP-Agent lies on the cost–accuracy efficiency frontier, and ablations show that each component primarily affects its corresponding certificate quantity.

Keywords: 
competitive programming, large language models, agentic reasoning, execution feedback, code generation

1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) now perform well across a broad range of downstream tasks, including code generation and everyday software-engineering assistance. Contest-level competitive programming (CP), however, remains a sharp failure case: on ICPC/IOI-style benchmarks (Jain et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026), even strong LLMs reach below 30% Pass@1 (Section 4). CP is judged by hidden correctness and asymptotic feasibility under strict time and memory limits, so plausible implementations earn no credit when the algorithm or an edge case is wrong, and software-engineering virtues such as maintainability or modular design do not compensate.

Recent work has explored two directions: (i) tackling competitive programming problems through massive code generation combined with heuristic-based inference and execution-based pruning, exemplified by AlphaCode (Li et al., 2022), AlphaCode2 (Leblond et al., 2023), and o1-ioi (El-Kishky et al., 2025); (ii) enhancing the intrinsic reasoning ability of LLMs, including large reasoning models (Guo et al., 2025; El-Kishky et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2025b; Liu et al., 2025) that are often trained with reinforcement learning. While these directions improve performance, they often come with substantial computational cost-large-scale sampling during inference, or expensive rollouts during training.

CP offers rich, executable feedback: compilation errors, test failures, and counterexamples directly expose concrete failure modes (Shinn et al., 2023). This makes agentic solving a natural fit. Two gaps, however, remain for agentic CP. First, the literature disagrees on which mechanisms reliably help. MapCoder (Islam et al., 2024) reports that additional test-case generation is unhelpful while AlphaCodium (Ridnik et al., 2024) reports gains; MapCoder and Oi-Assistant (Yuhua et al., 2025) find retrieval of similar problems useful, while AlgoSimBench (Li and Mooney, 2025) finds it unstable. Second, recent strong agentic CP systems increasingly invest in multi-stage agentic post-training (Team et al., 2026). In contrast, for training-free LLM agents on CP, it remains unclear whether tool orchestration alone improves performance and which mechanisms drive its gains.

These gaps converge to one essential question: which controllable mechanisms turn execution feedback into measurable gains on contest-level CP? We answer it through a calibrated risk-control view of feedback-driven solving. We analyze feedback-driven CP solving as a calibrated, risk-controlled stopped process. Its state reduces to three certificate quantities: the residual bad-candidate envelope ρt\rho_{t}, the accumulated program-level evidence ItI_{t}, and the active-state success hazard h¯t\underline{h}_{t}. Each is moved by exactly one abstract action class: RiskProbe on ρt\rho_{t}, EvidenceAcquire on ItI_{t}, and ContextAcquire on h¯t\underline{h}_{t}. The calibrated false-admission UCB q¯t≈ρ¯t​exp⁡(−ℐt)\bar{q}_{t}\approx\bar{\rho}_{t}\exp(-\mathcal{I}_{t}) follows as a derived quantity. This one-to-one reduction yields a unified design-and-selection framework: for any pre-declared finite manifest of controllers, it supplies a post-selection-valid lower bound on clean-before-false success. Guided by this framework, we design CP-Agent with one controller per action class: Dual-Granularity Verification contracts ρt\rho_{t}, Test Augmentation adds to ItI_{t}, and Experience-Driven Self-Evolving raises h¯t\underline{h}_{t}. A frozen admission gate and a refinement loop complete the agent. Extensive empirical results across three backbones on two contest-level benchmarks, together with theory-grounded mechanism ablations on the five-controller calibration class, jointly validate CP-Agent’s effectiveness and its calibrated certificate.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    A calibrated risk-control theory for feedback-driven CP. We prove an admission-risk theorem and a simultaneously valid finite-manifest selection rule over five abstract action classes (Section 2).

  • •

    A theory-induced agent. We instantiate this controller as CP-Agent, a tool-using framework with no parameter updates (Section 3).11 1 Our implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/NineAbyss/CP-Agent.

  • •

    Trace-calibrated mechanism evidence. On LiveCodeBench Pro and ICPC-Eval across three backbones, CP-Agent raises Pass@1 from 25.8% to 48.5% and Refine@5 by +11.0+11.0%; calibration attributes the gains to TA (evidence), HP (bad-plan survival), and Experience (success hazard) (Section 4).

2. A Calibrated Risk-Controlled Theory of Feedback Control

A feedback-driven CP agent repeatedly faces the same decision: admit the current candidate, refine it, or acquire more information. We specify certificate quantities that audit this decision, abstract action classes that act on them, and a calibration rule that turns them into a frozen controller; the takeaway box summarizes the role of the analysis and Appendix B consolidates the Section 2 notation.

Definition 2.1 (Controlled stopped process and certificate state).

Fix a horizon TT, false-admission budget α\alpha, and a frozen policy π\pi. Throughout, “step tt” denotes a refinement step—one response–revision attempt (one Refine advance, equivalently one outer-loop iteration of Algorithm 1), matched to Refine@KK and Pass@11. Within-trajectory interaction events such as individual LLM outputs or tool calls are termed interaction steps and appear only in diagnostic figures (e.g., Figure 3(a)). Before refinement step tt, the trajectory is active when At={τS>t−1,τF>t−1}A_{t}=\{\tau_{S}>t-1,\tau_{F}>t-1\}. On active trajectories, the implementation state is XtX_{t} (problem text, candidate code, feedback, retrieved memory, and tool outputs). The certificate exposes a lower-dimensional summary state

Zt:=ϕ⁡(Xt)=(ρt,It,h¯t,t),Z_{t}:=\phi(X_{t})=(\rho_{t},I_{t},\underline{h}_{t},t),

where ρt\rho_{t} is an upper envelope on residual bad-candidate mass, ItI_{t} is accumulated program-level evidence, and h¯t\underline{h}_{t} is a lower envelope on clean-success hazard. The residual admission-risk score is

(1) rt​(Zt):=ρt​exp⁡(−It).r_{t}(Z_{t}):=\rho_{t}\exp(-I_{t}).

Let Γt∈{0,1}\Gamma_{t}\in\{0,1\} denote the controller’s observable admission gate at step tt, the binary admit/reject signal logged on every active trace. If the controller admits a candidate through gate Γt\Gamma_{t}, hidden adjudication defines

Assumption 2.3 (Held-out exchangeability).

Calibration and evaluation problem trajectories are independent draws from the same benchmark distribution. Independence is required across problem trajectories at a fixed step tt; it is not required across refinement steps within a trajectory.

The controller manifest is

Controller certificate.

Theorem 2.5 controls risk-threshold stopping when a score threshold is part of the manifest, and audits the frozen observable gate otherwise. To select information-acquisition actions, we compare two separately calibrated UCBs on the active false-admission hazard — the raw bound from admitted-failure counts and the mechanism-factorized bound that multiplies probe-survival and evidence-gate-survival rates — and take their minimum (the mechanism factor wins when the probe and evidence channel together reject most of the bad mass; the raw bound wins when calibration data is sparse, since unfit mechanism factors fall back to 11):

q¯t,mechπ\displaystyle\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{mech}}^{\pi} =ρ¯tprobe,π​exp⁡[−ℐtevid,π],\displaystyle=\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi}\exp\!\bigl[-\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi}\bigr],

Here q¯t,rawπ\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{raw}}^{\pi} is the Clopper–Pearson UCB on qtπq_{t}^{\pi} from active calibration trajectories. Theorem 2.6 (Simultaneously valid finite-manifest calibration).

Let Πα\Pi_{\alpha} be a finite, pre-declared class of frozen controllers generated from the abstract action classes in Eq. (2); each controller maps certificate states to stop/refine decisions, model-controlled risk-probe calls, evidence intensity mm, context intensity kk, prompts, routing/deduplication rules, decoding parameters, a retrievable memory snapshot M⋆M^{\star}, and write mode ωwrite\omega_{\rm write}. Allocate the calibration failure probability δ\delta across the joint family of UCB/LCB statements as

δ=δraw+δgate+δprobe+δevid,\delta=\delta_{\mathrm{raw}}+\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}+\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}+\delta_{\mathrm{evid}},

with the per-component per-step splitting of Section 2 applied for each π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha} separately when estimating Eq. (7), Eq. (9), and Eq. (10). The calibrated selection rule is

(12) π⋆∈arg⁡maxπ∈Πα​CTctrl​(π).\pi^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha}}C_{T}^{\rm ctrl}(\pi).

Then, by a single union bound over Πα\Pi_{\alpha}, threshold grids, mechanism factors, and steps, with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta over calibration the UCBs/LCBs in Eq. (11) are simultaneously valid for every π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha}. Consequently, any π⋆\pi^{\star} selected by Eq. (12)—and any pre-declared frozen π\pi—inherits a post-selection-valid lower bound CTctrl​(π⋆)C_{T}^{\rm ctrl}(\pi^{\star}); if its manifest includes a score-threshold admission rule, the threshold also satisfies Theorem 2.5.

3. Method

Motivation & Overview.

CP-Agent is the instantiation of the selected controller π⋆\pi^{\star}: each abstract action class maps to a concrete tool (Table 1). All manifest entries—prompts, the observable admission gate, the HP and TA interfaces, the retrieval budget, the historical memory snapshot M⋆M^{\star}, the write mode, and the maximum horizon—are frozen before benchmark evaluation, either pre-declared or audited on held-out traces DcalD_{\rm cal} via Theorem 2.6.

3.1. Dual-Granularity Verification

RiskProbe and EvidenceAcquire​(m)\textsf{EvidenceAcquire}(m) act at different granularities: the former screens a reasoning state before it is admitted, the latter gates a complete candidate before it is trusted. CP-Agent realizes them as a Hypothesis Prober for the logged upstream gate GtHPG_{t}^{\mathrm{HP}} and a Solution Validator for the program-level admission screen inside Γt\Gamma_{t}. Separating the two roles prevents the upstream screen from being double-counted as calibrated program-level evidence.

Hypothesis Prober.

During early-stage reasoning, the agent often needs to verify local claims that are hard to establish purely in natural language—e.g., whether a recurrence holds on random small instances, whether a greedy rule fails on a constructed counterexample, or whether an invariant is preserved by a transition. CP-Agent exposes a Hypothesis Prober that compiles and runs short C++ snippets for this purpose. Under the frozen prompt and decoding policy the backbone itself decides when to call HP from its observable reasoning state—no hand-written trigger grid—and every call/pass/fail outcome is logged for calibration. A surviving HP call contracts the posterior odds of an upstream reasoning error (Proposition 2.7) and tightens the residual envelope ρ¯tprobe,π\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi} entering Eq. (9); HP thus moves ρt\rho_{t} (and the aggregate q¯t\bar{q}_{t}) alone, not the program-level evidence channel.

Solution Validator.

Once the agent produces a complete candidate implementation, the Solution Validator compiles and runs it against the local test suite: any public/local failure rejects the candidate and returns counterexample-level feedback. By default SV is a deterministic hard screen and contributes no calibrated statistical evidence; only when the suite uses fresh sampled tests or an externally calibrated set is an all-pass event additionally folded into ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} as the binary survival channel of Proposition 2.8.

3.2. Test Augmentation

The action class EvidenceAcquire​(m)\textsf{EvidenceAcquire}(m) makes the admission gate more informative against public-test-passing errors and exposes the evidence-acquisition intensity as a frozen controller entry. Public test suites 𝒯basic\mathcal{T}_{\text{basic}} are fixed and shallow, so passing them is a weak certificate: candidates routinely clear 𝒯basic\mathcal{T}_{\text{basic}} yet fail hidden tests in corner regimes. Test Augmentation (TA) instantiates EvidenceAcquire by appending consensus-filtered checks beyond 𝒯basic\mathcal{T}_{\text{basic}}; an all-pass on the augmented suite enters ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} as the binary survival channel of Proposition 2.8.

Augmentation pipeline.

CP-Agent implements test augmentation via three stages. Input Synthesis. Given the statement, the agent synthesizes a C++ input generator based on testlib.h22 2 https://github.com/MikeMirzayanov/testlib and command suites that sweep corner regimes such as min/max values, degenerate structures, adversarial patterns, and random sizes. Oracle Labeling. Ignoring time and memory limits often makes it easier to write a correct brute-force solver than an efficient one (Ridnik et al., 2024; He et al., 2025); CP-Agent therefore executes independently generated brute-force solvers on synthesized inputs to obtain candidate reference outputs. Consensus Filtering. Because brute-force programs can still be imperfect, CP-Agent runs multiple solvers in parallel and majority-votes their outputs. Candidates are evaluated on augmented tests only after passing public tests, so augmentation serves as additional diagnostic evidence after the basic admission screen. Budget and retries. The frozen TA manifest caps synthesis at 32 candidate augmented inputs per problem. This is an upper bound rather than a fixed suite size: the generator does not keep sampling until a nonempty suite is obtained, and there is no separate retention cap after filtering. Instead, CP-Agent retains all valid inputs that pass synthesis, compilation/execution, and consensus labeling within the cap; generator synthesis/compilation/execution may be retried up to five times. Consequently, GenRate measures the fraction of problems for which this capped protocol yields a nonempty suite, while the candidate-level evidence calibration treats the resulting suite as one binary survival channel.

3.3. Experience-Driven Self-Evolving

The action class ContextAcquire​(k)\textsf{ContextAcquire}(k) calls for a compact context prior MM that raises the active-state success hazard h¯t​(M)\underline{h}_{t}(M) in Corollary 2.10. A naive instantiation—continuously updating MM across the entire problem stream—would let target-split outcomes leak into MM and invalidate the calibration premise of Theorem 2.6: the hazard lift would no longer be data-independent of the evaluation split. CP-Agent resolves this with a temporal frozen-memory protocol,

Dhistmem→Dcal→Dtest.D_{\rm hist}^{\rm mem}\rightarrow D_{\rm cal}\rightarrow D_{\rm test}.

In memory-building mode, validated fail-to-pass traces from DhistmemD_{\rm hist}^{\rm mem} are written into a retrievable memory bank. In certificate-evaluation mode, the resulting snapshot M⋆M^{\star} is frozen before DcalD_{\rm cal} and DtestD_{\rm test}; both read M⋆M^{\star} read-only, and target-split experiences are written only to the audit log, never retrieved by subsequent target problems. Dataset instantiation of Dhistmem/Dcal/DtestD_{\rm hist}^{\rm mem}/D_{\rm cal}/D_{\rm test} is reported in §4.

Memory-building stage.

Notation. On Dhistmem=(q1,…,qn)D_{\rm hist}^{\rm mem}=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{n}) we index problems by rr and within-problem attempts by tt; the target-split index i∈Dcal∪Dtesti\in D_{\rm cal}\cup D_{\rm test} is disjoint from rr.

The design question is what evidence each experience should carry so that the resulting prior can move the hazard but not the calibration premise. We require each retrievable item to be a self-contained Fail→\toPass triplet—a failed attempt, its observable failure evidence, and a later observable passing correction on the same problem. The triplet anchors every learnt pattern to an observable counterexample, so retrieval at evaluation time substitutes for an additional probe rather than supplying labels; and because it is built only on DhistmemD_{\rm hist}^{\rm mem}, it leaves the active-row denominator ntπn_{t}^{\pi} on DcalD_{\rm cal} untouched.

Concretely, on problem qrq_{r} the agent maintains a build-time memory state MrbuildM^{\rm build}_{r} distilled from validated fixes. Candidate solutions are generated as

(16) sr,t=Gen⁡(qr,Mrbuild,hr,t−1),s_{r,t}=\mathrm{Gen}(q_{r},M^{\rm build}_{r},h_{r,t-1}),

where hr,t−1h_{r,t-1} summarizes within-problem history. The Solution Validator returns a pass indicator and public/local feedback,

(17) (vr,t,fr,t)=Φ⁡(qr,sr,t),vr,t∈{0,1},(v_{r,t},\,f_{r,t})=\Phi(q_{r},s_{r,t}),\qquad v_{r,t}\in\{0,1\},

with fr,tf_{r,t} the actionable failure feedback (unused when vr,t=1v_{r,t}{=}1), matching the (v,f)←Φ⁡(⋅)(v,f)\leftarrow\Phi(\cdot) call in Algorithm 1. For any failing attempt tt, define the first later observable pass

(18) t+​(r,t):=min⁡{u>t∣vr,u=1},t^{+}(r,t):=\min\{u>t\mid v_{r,u}=1\},

when it exists. The extracted experience is

(19) er,t=Exp⁡(qr,sr,t,sr,t+​(r,t),fr,t),e_{r,t}=\mathrm{Exp}(q_{r},s_{r,t},s_{r,t^{+}(r,t)},f_{r,t}),

(20) Mr+1build=Update⁡(Mrbuild,er,t).M^{\rm build}_{r+1}=\mathrm{Update}(M^{\rm build}_{r},e_{r,t}).

Because both sr,t+​(r,t)s_{r,t^{+}(r,t)} and fr,tf_{r,t} are observable on DhistmemD_{\rm hist}^{\rm mem}, no hidden label from Dcal∪DtestD_{\rm cal}\cup D_{\rm test} enters Exp⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Exp}(\cdot), Update⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Update}(\cdot), prompts, or routing.

Frozen certificate-evaluation stage.

After historical memory construction, calibration chooses a snapshot M⋆M^{\star} and controller manifest π⋆\pi^{\star} using DcalD_{\rm cal} with memory fixed. For every target calibration and test problem,

(21) Mitarget≡M⋆,i∈Dcal∪Dtest.M_{i}^{\rm target}\equiv M^{\star},\qquad i\in D_{\rm cal}\cup D_{\rm test}.

An extractable target-split experience is recorded only in an audit log M~\widetilde{M} for optional post-benchmark deployment:

(22) M~i+1=M~i∪{ei},Mi+1target=M⋆.\widetilde{M}_{i+1}=\widetilde{M}_{i}\cup\{e_{i}\},\qquad M_{i+1}^{\rm target}=M^{\star}.

Thus the calibrated certificate’s memory prior is data-independent of the target evaluation outcomes—exactly the i.i.d.-given-controller premise that Theorem 2.6 requires of the held-out rows.

Experience Curation.

The hazard lift attributable to MM is bounded by the description length of the retrieved evidence (Proposition 2.9), so curation is the part of the manifest that directly determines how much h¯t\underline{h}_{t} can move. We design three controllers, one per MDL component, and freeze all three into the manifest (Definition 2.4):

(i) Routing restricts the active hypothesis bucket by splitting the snapshot into two repositories, M⋆:=(ℳgen,ℳalg)M^{\star}:=(\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{gen}},\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{alg}}), where ℳgen\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{gen}} collects task-agnostic debugging patterns and ℳτ1,τ2alg\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{alg}}_{\tau_{1},\tau_{2}} is indexed by a two-level taxonomy (τ1,τ2)(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}) with 8 primary categories and 68 secondary tags.

(ii) LLM-mediated deduplication merges redundant traces: on each insertion the curation prompt compares the candidate against existing summaries in the target bank and rejects entries judged duplicate or covered by an existing generalization, so retrieved memory carries non-redundant evidence rather than near-copies of the same pattern.

(iii) Capacity controls the description length of retrieved memory by capping each bank, |ℳgen|≤20|\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{gen}}|\leq 20 and |ℳτ1,τ2alg|≤K=10|\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{alg}}_{\tau_{1},\tau_{2}}|\leq K{=}10; once a bank is at capacity the same semantic rule keeps at most the allowed number of representative experiences,

ℬ←Dedup⁡(ℬ,K).\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathrm{Dedup}(\mathcal{B};K).
Experience Utilization.

At evaluation time the two repositories play distinct roles in the hazard. The general bank supplies a task-agnostic prior shift applied to every problem: a compact summary is appended to the system prompt,

SysPrompti=\displaystyle\textsf{SysPrompt}_{i}={} BaseSysPrompt
∥Format(ℳgen,kgen),\displaystyle\|\ \mathrm{Format}(\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{gen}},k_{\text{gen}}),

raising the baseline component of h¯t​(M⋆)\underline{h}_{t}(M^{\star}) uniformly across qiq_{i}. The algorithmic bank supplies a task-conditional lift that fires only when qiq_{i} is routed to a populated bucket: CP-Agent predicts a taxonomy label and retrieves the corresponding frozen bucket,

(23a) (τ^1,τ^2)\displaystyle(\hat{\tau}_{1},\hat{\tau}_{2}) =ClassifyAlg⁡(qi),\displaystyle=\mathrm{ClassifyAlg}(q_{i}),
(23b) Eialg\displaystyle E_{i}^{\mathrm{alg}} =RetrieveAlgExp⁡(τ^1,τ^2,ℓ,M⋆),\displaystyle=\mathrm{RetrieveAlgExp}(\hat{\tau}_{1},\hat{\tau}_{2};\ell,M^{\star}),

contributing the residual, problem-specific portion of the lift. Both pathways read M⋆M^{\star} read-only, so the realized hazard h¯tπ​(M⋆)\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star}) remains the calibrated quantity entering Corollary 2.10, and the refinement-step-11 (t=1t{=}1) acceptance gain in Table 5 is its empirical instantiation.

3.4. Tool Orchestration

CP-Agent runs a stage-wise refinement loop coordinating the three components. For each problem qiq_{i}, the system prompt is initialized with the general bank of M⋆M^{\star} and, when helpful, retrieved algorithmic experiences EialgE_{i}^{\mathrm{alg}}. The frozen backbone then drafts a solution and may call the Hypothesis Prober to falsify local hypotheses before committing; the Solution Validator compiles and runs each draft on public tests, whose feedback drives subsequent edits; once all public tests pass, Test Augmentation generates consensus-filtered cases. In deployment mode, attempts may be appended to retrievable memory via Eq. (20); in certificate-evaluation mode they are written only to the audit log M~\widetilde{M} via Eq. (22). The mapping to the abstract controller of Section 2 is direct: HP →RiskProbe\to\textsf{RiskProbe}, SV/TA →EvidenceAcquire​(m)\to\textsf{EvidenceAcquire}(m), Experience →ContextAcquire​(k)\to\textsf{ContextAcquire}(k). Algorithm 1 gives the full loop, with an outer loop over the TT refinement steps of Def. 2.1 and an inner loop over within-step HP probes (the interaction steps of Fig. 3(a)), so a single refinement step—including T=1T{=}1 on LCB-Pro—can host many HP calls before the candidate is committed.

4. Experiment

4.1. Experiment Setup

Backbone LLMs

To evaluate the general applicability of our method across different LLMs, we conducted experiments using three distinct backbone LLMs: GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024), Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025), and DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat (Liu et al., 2025) for all multi-agent workflows and CP-Agent variants.

Baselines

We compare against two baseline groups: (i) Frontier LLMs: DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025), DeepSeek-V3.2-Reasoner (Liu et al., 2025), Gemini-3-pro (Pichai et al., 2025), and o4-mini-high (OpenAI, 2025b). (ii) Agent frameworks/workflows: For a fair comparison, we evaluate three agent frameworks: Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), CodeSim (Islam et al., 2025), and AlphaCodium (Ridnik et al., 2024), each with the same three backbones, all targeting C++.

Evaluation datasets.

We evaluate all baselines and CP-Agent variants on two competition-style, contamination-controlled benchmarks: LiveCodeBench Pro (Zheng et al., 2026) and ICPC-Eval (Xu et al., 2026). The target split for LCB-Pro is the held-out 2025Q2 subset. The temporal partition that Experience uses on LCB-Pro and the controller transfer to ICPC-Eval are described in §4.2 (summarized in Table 3).

Metrics

For ICPC-Eval, we use Refine@K (Xu et al., 2026) to measure iterative refinement under execution feedback, i.e., whether the model passes the hidden judge within KK response–revision attempts; we report Refine@5 (K=5K{=}5) to reflect the interactive nature of competitive programming. For LiveCodeBench Pro, we report Pass@1 to match its standard single-shot setting and prior work, and use per-refinement-step analyses (t=1,2,3t{=}1,2,3) when studying the role of experience.

Implementations.

The full frozen controller manifest—refinement horizon TT, retrieval budgets (kgen,ℓalg)(k_{\rm gen},\ell_{\rm alg}), TA intensity mm and consensus rule γevid\gamma_{\rm evid}, decoding parameters, and prompt template—is given in Table 3. Baselines (Reflexion, CodeSim, AlphaCodium) use their official prompts and control flow with the same three backbones. HP, TA, and Experience are added only inside CP-Agent variants and never touch baselines.

4.2. Calibration Protocol and Auditability

The controller is calibrated before final benchmark reporting and is never recomputed after observing evaluation outcomes. We use a temporal three-stage protocol,

Dhistmem→Dcal→Dtest.D_{\rm hist}^{\rm mem}\rightarrow D_{\rm cal}\rightarrow D_{\rm test}.

First, the 387 historical pre-test problems in biannual_2024_7_12 construct candidate memory snapshots through the memory-building rule in Eq. (20). Second, for each candidate policy π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha}, we run the frozen agent with a fixed snapshot M⋆M^{\star} on the disjoint 166-problem calibration split quater_2025_1_3, record every active trace row, compute the one-sided bounds in Eq. (7), audit the observable admission gate using Eq. (8), and select the best declared manifest from Πα\Pi_{\alpha} by Eq. (12). Third, final benchmark runs on DtestD_{\rm test} use the selected controller in certificate-evaluation mode: the policy, memory snapshot, TA consensus threshold, HP tool interface, prompts, decoding parameters, maximum horizon, and write mode are frozen, and target-test experiences are written only to the audit log but not retrievable. For ICPC-Eval we transfer the LCB-Pro–selected controller and the same frozen snapshot M⋆M^{\star} directly to the ICPC target split, under the identical certificate-evaluation mode.

Hidden-judge outcomes are used in calibration only as labels for StS_{t} and FtF_{t} after a candidate has passed the observable gate Γt\Gamma_{t}; they are not exposed to the agent during refinement and are never used for target-split memory writes, retrieval, prompt updates, routing, or controller selection. This separation is important: public/local execution can guide repair, whereas hidden outcomes define the calibration labels for the stopped-process certificate. A trace contributes to the denominator ntn_{t} only if it is active at step tt; a candidate that fails SV or TA contributes neither to sts_{t} nor to ftf_{t} because it was not admitted. These conventions align the empirical hazards with Definition 2.1 and the admission risk with Theorem 2.5.

4.3. Main Results

From Table 2: (1) CP-Agent improves consistently across backbones, with best gains on DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat of +11.0+11.0 (ICPC-Eval Refine@5) and +22.7+22.7 (LCB-Pro Pass@1, 81/16781/167 vs. 43/16743/167, Wilson 95% CIs non-overlapping); (2) it matches or beats same-backbone baselines and equals DeepSeek-V3.2-Reasoner on ICPC-Eval at 33.933.9 Refine@5 under frozen memory; (3) gains scale with backbone strength. Section 4.4 audits Corollary 2.10’s clean component.

4.4. Trace-Calibrated Certificate and Mechanism Evidence

We instantiate the certificate on a held-out calibration split using the logging schema in Definition 2.1. The pre-declared manifest class is Πα={Base,+SV,+SV+HP,+SV+HP+TA,Full}\Pi_{\alpha}=\{\text{Base},\,\text{+SV},\,\text{+SV+HP},\,\text{+SV+HP+TA},\,\text{Full}\} (|Πα|=5|\Pi_{\alpha}|=5); each controller is evaluated on DcalD_{\rm cal} with the per-controller-split Clopper–Pearson allocations of the Numerical instantiation paragraph, and Eq. (12) selects the one with the largest CTctrl​(π)C_{T}^{\rm ctrl}(\pi) for final evaluation. Table 4 reports the theorem-level products and certificate values; compact display rates are derived from these products and are not homogeneous-step assumptions.

Table 4 shows that the certificate ranking matches the ablation trend: the Full temporal frozen-memory controller has the largest C5ctrl​(π)C^{\rm ctrl}_{5}(\pi), and C5ctrl​(π)C^{\rm ctrl}_{5}(\pi) lies below the matched-horizon ICPC-Eval Refine@5 in every row, as required. Mechanism calibration on the 166-problem calibration split gives: HP odds contraction σ¯tbad/σ¯tgood=0.46/0.71=0.65\bar{\sigma}_{t}^{\rm bad}/\underline{\sigma}_{t}^{\rm good}=0.46/0.71=0.65, with σ¯tbad\bar{\sigma}_{t}^{\rm bad} the Clopper–Pearson UCB on σtbad\sigma_{t}^{\rm bad} (Proposition 2.7) and σ¯tgood\underline{\sigma}_{t}^{\rm good} the LCB on the analogous good-plan rate Pr⁡(Wtprobe=1∣¬Btϵ,At)\Pr(W_{t}^{\rm probe}{=}1\mid\neg B_{t}^{\epsilon},A_{t}); TA evidence increment Δ​It​(m=32)=−log⁡b¯t​(m=32)=1.00\Delta I_{t}(m{=}32)=-\log\bar{b}_{t}(m{=}32)=1.00 nats with post-survival bug rate 11/58=19.0%11/58=19.0\% on the 117-candidate diagnostic pool. For Experience, Table 5 reports cumulative judge-acceptance with and without the frozen snapshot M⋆M^{\star} over the first three refinement steps on both benchmarks. The refinement step tt is the response–revision attempt of Definition 2.1, and we operationalize it per benchmark: on LCB-Pro, tt indexes the tt-th Solution Validator admission within a trajectory—the per-step counterpart of the single-shot Pass@1 protocol (T=1T{=}1 in Table 3)—while on ICPC-Eval, tt indexes the tt-th official judge submission under the Refine@5 protocol. Each cell is the fraction of DcalD_{\rm cal} problems whose first judge-accepted submission arrives by step tt; both w/ Exp rows read the same pre-built M⋆M^{\star}, so the comparison isolates Experience and is order-independent. The lift concentrates at t=1t{=}1 (+9.6+9.6 pp on LCB-Pro and +3.4+3.4 pp on ICPC-Eval) and shrinks at later steps, consistent with ContextAcquire acting on the active-state hazard h¯t​(M)\underline{h}_{t}(M) in Proposition 2.9 rather than on ρ¯tprobe\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\rm probe} or ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}.

4.5. Efficiency Analysis

We analyze cost–performance trade-offs with the variable-returns-to-scale Banker–Charnes–Cooper DEA model (Charnes et al., 1978; Banker et al., 1984) (input == Cost, output == Pass@1; θ=1\theta{=}1 marks the BCC-efficient frontier). Figure 1 shows that CP-Agent lies on the frontier for all three backbones (DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat, GPT-4o, Qwen3-235B), whereas baselines such as Reflexion are on the frontier only on some backbones (DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat) and dominated on others (Qwen3-235B). On DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat, agentic baselines and CP-Agent all sit in the 10−210^{-2} USD per-problem range (CP-Agent: $0.0350.035, Table 4); the frontier is therefore driven by CP-Agent’s higher Pass@1 at comparable cost rather than by an order-of-magnitude cost gap. Tracked components account for 92.4%92.4\% of total cost (HP 69.7%69.7\%, SV 17.6%17.6\%, Experience 3.4%3.4\%, TA 1.7%1.7\%).

4.6. Tool-Use Analysis

We analyze how CP-Agent’s tool use affects the three quantities identified by the theory: false-admission risk, calibrated admission evidence, and experience-conditioned success hazard.

Dual-Granularity Verification.

Figure 3(a) (LCB-Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat) shows that, indexed by interaction step (the ii-th in-trajectory LLM/tool event, distinct from refinement step tt in Definition 2.1), HP peaks at the first few steps and decays as the approach stabilizes, while SV stays roughly uniform—early hypothesis checks, then solution-level validation on executable candidates.

Test Augmentation.

Let GenRateaug\mathrm{GenRate}_{\rm aug} be the fraction of problems with a non-empty TA suite, and call problem ii rescued if a public-passing candidate that initially failed augmented tests later passes them and is accepted. Figure 3(b) reports these on the 167-problem target split: GPT-4o reaches GenRateaug=39.5%\mathrm{GenRate}_{\rm aug}{=}39.5\% vs. Qwen3-235B-A22B 68.3%68.3\% and DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat 70.1%70.1\%, mainly reflecting brute-force quality; RescueRateaug\mathrm{RescueRate}_{\rm aug} is substantial across backbones (9.39.3–23.9%23.9\%), with DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat highest, indicating that both test strength and the backbone’s ability to act on feedback matter. Both diagnostics map to the evidence variable of Proposition 2.8: GenRateaug\mathrm{GenRate}_{\rm aug} is the availability of the evidence channel (𝒯aug≠∅\mathcal{T}_{\rm aug}\neq\emptyset, required for b¯tπ​(m)\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}(m) to be informative), and RescueRateaug\mathrm{RescueRate}_{\rm aug} tracks the “counterexample-found” rate that tightens b¯tπ​(m)\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}(m); §4.4 converts this to Δ​It​(m=32)≈1.00\Delta I_{t}(m{=}32){\approx}1.00 nats in Table 4.

Experience-Driven Self-Evolving

Certificate-bearing benchmark results use the temporal frozen snapshot protocol in Section 4.2: historical problems build M⋆M^{\star}, calibration audits the controller with M⋆M^{\star} fixed, and final testing reads the same snapshot. Deployment-mode growth diagnostics in the full study show that general experiences saturate quickly while algorithmic memories keep expanding as new problem types appear; the curriculum effect follows our write-in criterion, because experiences are stored only after a failure is repaired. These diagnostics explain snapshot construction on DhistmemD_{\rm hist}^{\rm mem}, while all reported certificates freeze the resulting snapshot before DcalD_{\rm cal} and DtestD_{\rm test}.

4.7. Ablation Study

Table 4 also serves as the component ablation on DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat: SV and HP constitute Dual-Granularity Verification, TA generates extra tests beyond public cases, and Exp retrieves reusable repair knowledge from past successful trajectories. Vanilla LLM yields 22.922.9 Refine@5 on ICPC-Eval and 25.825.8 Pass@1 on LCB-Pro at $0.002 per problem. Adding SV markedly improves both (31.4/43.731.4/43.7 at $0.023); SV+HP further improves to 32.2/44.332.2/44.3, supporting their complementarity. Adding TA on top of Dual-Granularity Verification brings additional Pass@1 gains at higher cost (33.1/46.133.1/46.1 at $0.043). Finally, historical frozen Experience achieves the best performance (33.9/48.533.9/48.5) and reduces per-problem cost back to $0.035, indicating that retrieved repair experiences reduce ineffective trial-and-error without using calibration- or test-split write-ins. The certificate column C5ctrlC_{5}^{\rm ctrl} rises monotonically with the same component additions, so the ablation ranking reproduces the certificate ranking on DcalD_{\rm cal}.

Additional diagnostics.

TA reliability on 117 public-pass candidates: TA flags 40/51 hidden-wrong programs while letting 47/66 hidden-correct survive, leaving the 11/58=19.0%11/58{=}19.0\% post-survival bug rate used by Prop. 2.8; sampling kk tests per suite raises detection to 74.5%74.5\% at k=15k{=}15.

5. Related Work

Competitive programming agents.

Among tool-augmented LLM agents that ground reasoning on deterministic execution feedback (Yao et al., 2022; Madaan et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2022b; Gou et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Das et al., 2024), work on CP benchmarks (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Jain et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026) mostly raises accuracy by scale: dedicated training or massive sampling (Li et al., 2022; Leblond et al., 2023; El-Kishky et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). Inference-time pipelines such as MapCoder, AlphaCodium, and CodeSim avoid retraining by iterating generation and verification, but are session-local and discard repair experience after each problem (Islam et al., 2024; Ridnik et al., 2024; Islam et al., 2025; Yuhua et al., 2025; Li and Mooney, 2025). Reflexion-style self-refinement (Shinn et al., 2023) keeps verbal memory across problems but offers no admission rule for when retrieved memory should enter the loop. CP-Agent adds neither training nor sampling: a calibrated controller ties generation, verification, and a frozen memory snapshot to a single held-out audit, closing the gap to a stronger reasoner (Liu et al., 2025) on ICPC-Eval Refine@5.

Testing, risk control, and frozen memory.

Randomized testing and generated checks have long driven program repair and synthesis (Claessen and Hughes, 2000; Solar-Lezama et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2022a; He et al., 2025), but are usually consumed as raw signals. We treat SV and TA as calibrated evidence channels via binomial calibration, conformal-style risk control, and anytime-valid evidence (Clopper and Pearson, 1934; Angelopoulos et al., 2024; Howard et al., 2021; Vovk and Wang, 2021), so coverage and post-survival risk are read off held-out traces. Experience enters as a temporal frozen memory prior with PAC-Bayes/MDL complexity control (McAllester, 1999; McAllester, 1999): tools and memory are fixed on DhistmemD_{\rm hist}^{\rm mem} before DcalD_{\rm cal} and DtestD_{\rm test} (Section 4.2) so the audit remains valid; memory may still grow in deployment.

6. Conclusion

A calibrated risk-controlled controller substantially improves contest-level programming without additional training. The theory derives certificate quantities and abstract action classes that are audited on held-out traces and frozen before evaluation; CP-Agent instantiates them as Dual-Granularity Verification, Test Augmentation, and Experience-Driven Self-Evolving, matches DeepSeek-V3.2-Reasoner on ICPC-Eval Refine@5, and provides trace-calibrated mechanism evidence for each action class.

Appendix A Tool-Orchestrated Pseudocode

Algorithm 1 formalizes §3.4 with two nested loops: the outer loop indexes refinement steps t=1,…,Tt{=}1,\ldots,T (one admission each, matched to Refine@KK/Pass@1), and the inner loop indexes interaction steps within tt—HP probes consume interaction steps but not refinement steps, so a single tt (even T=1T{=}1 on LCB-Pro) can absorb many HP calls before Commit. Memory writes follow Def. 2.4 and uncalled channels record their gate as neutral (Def. 2.1).

Appendix C Section 2 Proofs

This appendix contains the proofs for Section 2 ("A Calibrated Risk-Controlled Theory of Feedback Control") of the paper, covering the calibration estimators after Definition 2.4, Theorem 2.5, Theorem 2.6, Propositions 2.7–2.9, Corollary 2.10, and the validity of the mechanism factorization in Eq. (9).

0. Setting and Conventions

0.1 Probability space and stopped events

Fix a frozen controller π\pi. A trajectory is generated by sampling one problem from the benchmark distribution and running π\pi for at most TT refinement steps. All probabilities Prπ⁡(⋅)\Pr_{\pi}(\cdot) are taken with respect to a fresh evaluation trajectory; calibration probabilities are taken with respect to held-out calibration trajectories.

The stopping times are

τF:=inf{t:Ft=1},τS:=inf{t:St=1},\tau_{F}:=\inf\{t:F_{t}=1\},\hskip 18.49988pt\tau_{S}:=\inf\{t:S_{t}=1\},

and the active event before step tt is

At:={τS>t−1,τF>t−1}.A_{t}:=\{\tau_{S}>t-1,\;\tau_{F}>t-1\}.

By Definition 2.1,

Ft:=𝟏​{At,Γt=1,Btϵ},St:=𝟏​{At,Γt=1,¬Btϵ},F_{t}:=\mathbf{1}\{A_{t},\,\Gamma_{t}=1,\,B_{t}^{\epsilon}\},\hskip 18.49988ptS_{t}:=\mathbf{1}\{A_{t},\,\Gamma_{t}=1,\,\neg B_{t}^{\epsilon}\},

so FtF_{t} and StS_{t} are mutually exclusive at every fixed step tt via BtϵB_{t}^{\epsilon}. Hence τS\tau_{S} and τF\tau_{F} cannot both be finite and equal (they may, however, both equal +∞+\infty when neither stop occurs by TT, with the convention inf∅:=+∞\inf\varnothing:=+\infty). The certified event is

{τS≤T,τS<τF}.\{\tau_{S}\leq T,\;\tau_{S}<\tau_{F}\}.

We adopt the stopped-process convention: once a clean success or false admission occurs at some step t⋆t^{\star}, StS_{t} and FtF_{t} are set to 00 at all subsequent steps t>t⋆t>t^{\star} and the trajectory is inactive. As a consequence, if τS<∞\tau_{S}<\infty then Ft=0F_{t}=0 for all t>τSt>\tau_{S}, so τF=+∞\tau_{F}=+\infty on {τS<τF}\{\tau_{S}<\tau_{F}\}; symmetrically, τS=+∞\tau_{S}=+\infty on {τF<τS}\{\tau_{F}<\tau_{S}\}. We further assume Prπ⁡(A1)=1\Pr_{\pi}(A_{1})=1, i.e., the trajectory begins active at step 11.

0.2 Admission-gate semantics required by the mechanism factorization

Eq. (9) and Section 5 below use the containment

{Ft=1}⊆{Btϵ=1,Wtprobe=1,Wtevid=1}on At.\{F_{t}=1\}\subseteq\{B_{t}^{\epsilon}=1,\;W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\;W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\}\hskip 9.24994pt\text{on }A_{t}.

This is equivalent to the requirement that the observable admission gate satisfies

Γt=1⟹Wtprobe=1​and​Wtevid=1​on ​At,\Gamma_{t}=1\;\Longrightarrow\;W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\;\text{and}\;W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\hskip 9.24994pt\text{on }A_{t},

i.e., any candidate released by Γt\Gamma_{t} has first passed the risk-probe and evidence stages (with the convention Wprobe=Wevid=1W^{\mathrm{probe}}=W^{\mathrm{evid}}=1 when the corresponding stage is not invoked). We treat this implication as part of the manifest contract on π\pi; if Γ1:Tobs\Gamma_{1:T}^{\mathrm{obs}} does not chain the upstream screens, the mechanism UCB is invalid and only the raw UCB q¯t,rawπ\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{raw}}^{\pi} applies.

0.3 Held-out exchangeability

Under Assumption 2.3, calibration and evaluation trajectories are independent draws from the same benchmark distribution. Independence is required across problem trajectories at a fixed step tt, not across refinement steps within a trajectory. For fixed tt and π\pi, the active calibration rows yield conditional Bernoulli samples; a random active denominator does not invalidate the bounds, because we condition on the denominator first and then mix.

0.4 Zero-probability conditioning

For any conditional probability Pr⁡(H∣E)\Pr(H\mid E) with Pr⁡(E)=0\Pr(E)=0, we set Pr⁡(H∣E):=0\Pr(H\mid E):=0. This convention never inflates an upper bound; in chain-rule decompositions, the corresponding event has probability 00 and contributes nothing.

0.5 Clopper–Pearson UCB / LCB

Let Y1,…,Yn​∼i.i.d.​Bernoulli​(p)Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p) and K=∑iYiK=\sum_{i}Y_{i}. Write

U⁡(K,n,η)=UCBBinom​(K,n,η),L⁡(K,n,η)=LCBBinom​(K,n,η)U(K,n,\eta)=\mathrm{UCB}_{\mathrm{Binom}}(K,n,\eta),\hskip 18.49988ptL(K,n,\eta)=\mathrm{LCB}_{\mathrm{Binom}}(K,n,\eta)

for the exact one-sided Clopper–Pearson bounds, so that

Prp{p≤U(K,n,η)}≥1−η,Prp{p≥L(K,n,η)}≥1−η.\Pr_{p}\{p\leq U(K,n,\eta)\}\geq 1-\eta,\hskip 18.49988pt\Pr_{p}\{p\geq L(K,n,\eta)\}\geq 1-\eta.

If the denominator NN is random with K|N=n∼Binomial⁡(n,p)K\mid N=n\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p), then

Pr{p>U(K,N,η)}=∑nPr(N=n)Pr{p>U(K,n,η)∣N=n}≤η,\Pr\{p>U(K,N,\eta)\}=\sum_{n}\Pr(N=n)\,\Pr\{p>U(K,n,\eta)\mid N=n\}\leq\eta,

and the analogous bound holds for the LCB. We use the conservative conventions

UCBBinom​(0,0,η)=1,LCBBinom​(0,0,η)=0.\mathrm{UCB}_{\mathrm{Binom}}(0,0,\eta)=1,\hskip 18.49988pt\mathrm{LCB}_{\mathrm{Binom}}(0,0,\eta)=0.

0.6 Pre-declaration of score-defining objects

The proof of Theorem 2.5 requires that the score function rt​(Zt)=ρt​exp⁡(−It)r_{t}(Z_{t})=\rho_{t}\exp(-I_{t}), the finite threshold grid Θt\Theta_{t} (with 1≤|Θt|<∞1\leq|\Theta_{t}|<\infty), and the gate rule 𝟏{rt≤θ}\mathbf{1}\{r_{t}\leq\theta\} be determined by π\pi alone, using only the observable trajectory state. Concretely:

  1. (1)

    The measurable map ϕπ:Xt↦Zt=(ρt,It,h¯t,t)\phi_{\pi}:X_{t}\mapsto Z_{t}=(\rho_{t},I_{t},\underline{h}_{t},t) depends only on observable mechanism outputs (probe survival, evidence-gate survival, retrieval slots, step index), not on hidden labels BtϵB_{t}^{\epsilon}.

  2. (2)

    The finite grid Θt\Theta_{t} is determined by π\pi with 1≤|Θt|<∞1\leq|\Theta_{t}|<\infty.

  3. (3)

    The gate rule 𝟏{rt≤θ}\mathbf{1}\{r_{t}\leq\theta\} is determined by π\pi.

If ϕπ\phi_{\pi}, Θt\Theta_{t}, the aggregation rule γevid\gamma_{\mathrm{evid}}, the memory snapshot M⋆M^{\star}, or any calibrated scalar in rtr_{t} (such as ρ¯tprobe,π\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi} or b¯tπ\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}) is tuned on DcalD_{\mathrm{cal}}, every candidate value must be enumerated in the finite, pre-declared manifest class Πα\Pi_{\alpha} (with 1≤|Πα|<∞1\leq|\Pi_{\alpha}|<\infty) in advance, so that the union bound of Theorem 2.6 absorbs both the score selection and the gate threshold selection. Throughout Theorem 2.5 and Theorem 2.6 we treat this pre-declaration as a standing hypothesis.

1. Validity of the Calibration Estimators in Eq. (7)

For fixed π\pi and step tt, let ntπn_{t}^{\pi} be the number of active calibration rows, ftπf_{t}^{\pi} the count of false admissions, and stπs_{t}^{\pi} the count of clean successes. Define

q¯t,rawπ:=UCBBinom​(ftπ,ntπ,δ2​T),h¯tπ:=LCBBinom​(stπ,ntπ,δ2​T).\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{raw}}^{\pi}:=\mathrm{UCB}_{\mathrm{Binom}}\!\left(f_{t}^{\pi},n_{t}^{\pi},\tfrac{\delta}{2T}\right),\hskip 18.49988pt\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}:=\mathrm{LCB}_{\mathrm{Binom}}\!\left(s_{t}^{\pi},n_{t}^{\pi},\tfrac{\delta}{2T}\right).

The deployment hazards are qtπ:=Prπ⁡(Ft=1∣At)q_{t}^{\pi}:=\Pr_{\pi}(F_{t}=1\mid A_{t}) and htπ:=Prπ⁡(St=1∣At)h_{t}^{\pi}:=\Pr_{\pi}(S_{t}=1\mid A_{t}).

Proof. Fix tt and π\pi. Let Ai,tA_{i,t} be the active indicator for calibration trajectory ii. On {Ai,t=1}\{A_{i,t}=1\}, Fi,tF_{i,t} is Bernoulli with parameter qtπq_{t}^{\pi}. By Assumption 2.3, different trajectories are independent at fixed tt, so the active rows yield i.i.d. Bernoulli⁡(qtπ)\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q_{t}^{\pi}) samples; the random denominator ntπn_{t}^{\pi} is handled by Section 0.5. The Clopper–Pearson UCB gives

Pr{qtπ≤q¯t,rawπ}≥1−δ2​T.\Pr\{q_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{raw}}^{\pi}\}\geq 1-\tfrac{\delta}{2T}.

The same argument applied to Si,tS_{i,t} gives Pr{htπ≥h¯tπ}≥1−δ2​T\Pr\{h_{t}^{\pi}\geq\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}\}\geq 1-\tfrac{\delta}{2T}. A union bound over the 2​T2T one-sided events t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T yields

Pr⁡{∀t≤T:qtπ≤q¯t,rawπ​and​htπ≥h¯tπ}≥1−δ.□\Pr\!\left\{\forall t\leq T:\;q_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{raw}}^{\pi}\;\text{and}\;h_{t}^{\pi}\geq\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}\right\}\geq 1-\delta.\hskip 18.49988pt\square

The argument requires only across-trajectory independence at fixed tt, not within-trajectory step independence.

2. Theorem 2.5: Calibrated Admission Gate

Statement. Assume the pre-declaration of Section 0.6: ϕπ\phi_{\pi}, the score function rt​(Zt)=ρt​exp⁡(−It)r_{t}(Z_{t})=\rho_{t}\exp(-I_{t}), the finite non-empty grid Θt\Theta_{t} (with 1≤|Θt|<∞1\leq|\Theta_{t}|<\infty), and the gate rule are fixed by π\pi before label counting; any calibrated scalar entering rtr_{t} is enumerated in the finite, non-empty manifest Πα\Pi_{\alpha} (with 1≤|Πα|<∞1\leq|\Pi_{\alpha}|<\infty). On held-out calibration traces, let nt​(θ)n_{t}(\theta) be the number of active candidate admissions with rt​(Zt)≤θr_{t}(Z_{t})\leq\theta and ft​(θ)f_{t}(\theta) the count of such admissions rejected by hidden evaluation. Define

R¯t​(θ):=UCBBinom​(ft​(θ),nt​(θ),δgateT​|Θt|)\bar{R}_{t}(\theta):=\mathrm{UCB}_{\mathrm{Binom}}\!\left(f_{t}(\theta),\,n_{t}(\theta),\,\tfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}}{T|\Theta_{t}|}\right)

and select

θ^t,α=max⁡{θ∈Θt:R¯t​(θ)≤αt},\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha}=\max\{\theta\in\Theta_{t}:\bar{R}_{t}(\theta)\leq\alpha_{t}\},

with θ^t,α:=−∞\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha}:=-\infty and Γtα≡0\Gamma_{t}^{\alpha}\equiv 0 when the set is empty. Then, with calibration probability at least 1−δgate1-\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}, the gate Γtα=𝟏{rt(Zt)≤θ^t,α}\Gamma_{t}^{\alpha}=\mathbf{1}\{r_{t}(Z_{t})\leq\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha}\} satisfies

Pr⁡(Ft=1∣At,Γtα=1)≤αt\Pr(F_{t}=1\mid A_{t},\,\Gamma_{t}^{\alpha}=1)\leq\alpha_{t}

simultaneously for all t≤Tt\leq T and all data-dependent θ^t,α∈Θt\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha}\in\Theta_{t}.

Proof. Section 0.6 asserts that ϕπ\phi_{\pi}, Θt\Theta_{t}, and the gate rule are pre-declared (or absorbed into Πα\Pi_{\alpha} by Theorem 2.6). Fix tt and θ∈Θt\theta\in\Theta_{t}, and define the deployment conditional rejection rate

pt,θ:=Prπ⁡(Ft=1∣At,rt​(Zt)≤θ).p_{t,\theta}:=\Pr_{\pi}(F_{t}=1\mid A_{t},\,r_{t}(Z_{t})\leq\theta).

The conditioning event {At,rt​(Zt)≤θ}\{A_{t},\,r_{t}(Z_{t})\leq\theta\} is determined by observables. By Assumption 2.3, the calibration rows satisfying this event yield i.i.d. Bernoulli⁡(pt,θ)\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{t,\theta}) samples for hidden rejection, with a random denominator nt​(θ)n_{t}(\theta) handled by Section 0.5. The Clopper–Pearson UCB gives

Pr{pt,θ≤R¯t(θ)}≥1−δgateT​|Θt|.\Pr\{p_{t,\theta}\leq\bar{R}_{t}(\theta)\}\geq 1-\tfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}}{T|\Theta_{t}|}.

Union-bounding over t≤Tt\leq T and θ∈Θt\theta\in\Theta_{t} defines the good event

Ggate:={∀t≤T,∀θ∈Θt:pt,θ≤R¯t(θ)},Pr(Ggate)≥1−δgate.G_{\mathrm{gate}}:=\{\forall t\leq T,\,\forall\theta\in\Theta_{t}:\;p_{t,\theta}\leq\bar{R}_{t}(\theta)\},\hskip 9.24994pt\Pr(G_{\mathrm{gate}})\geq 1-\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}.

On GgateG_{\mathrm{gate}}, consider the data-dependent choice θ^t,α\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha}.

Case 1: the selection set is non-empty. Then θ^t,α∈Θt\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha}\in\Theta_{t} and R¯t​(θ^t,α)≤αt\bar{R}_{t}(\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha})\leq\alpha_{t}. Since GgateG_{\mathrm{gate}} holds at every grid point,

pt,θ^t,α≤R¯t​(θ^t,α)≤αt,p_{t,\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha}}\leq\bar{R}_{t}(\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha})\leq\alpha_{t},

and Γtα=1\Gamma_{t}^{\alpha}=1 is equivalent to rt​(Zt)≤θ^t,αr_{t}(Z_{t})\leq\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha}, so

Pr⁡(Ft=1∣At,Γtα=1)=pt,θ^t,α≤αt.\Pr(F_{t}=1\mid A_{t},\,\Gamma_{t}^{\alpha}=1)=p_{t,\hat{\theta}_{t,\alpha}}\leq\alpha_{t}.

Case 2: the selection set is empty. Then Γtα≡0\Gamma_{t}^{\alpha}\equiv 0, and Pr⁡(At,Γtα=1)=0\Pr(A_{t},\,\Gamma_{t}^{\alpha}=1)=0; by Section 0.4 the conditional probability is 0≤αt0\leq\alpha_{t}. □\hskip 18.49988pt\square

The post-selection validity follows from establishing the UCB simultaneously over the finite grid before any data-dependent choice is made.

3. Proposition 2.7: RiskProbe Bad-and-Survive UCB

Statement. Let Wtprobe∈{0,1}W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}\in\{0,1\} be the probe-survival indicator at step tt (set to 11 when the probe is not invoked). On held-out calibration traces, let ntπn_{t}^{\pi} be the number of active rows at step tt under π\pi, and let ftprobe,πf_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi} count those rows where both Btϵ=1B_{t}^{\epsilon}=1 and Wtprobe=1W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1. Define

ρ¯tprobe,π:=UCBBinom​(ftprobe,π,ntπ,δprobeT).\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi}:=\mathrm{UCB}_{\mathrm{Binom}}\!\left(f_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi},\,n_{t}^{\pi},\,\tfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}}{T}\right).

Then, with calibration probability at least 1−δprobe1-\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}, simultaneously for t≤Tt\leq T,

ρ¯tprobe,π≥Prπ⁡(Btϵ,Wtprobe=1∣At),\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi}\geq\Pr_{\pi}(B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\mid A_{t}),

and

Prπ⁡(Btϵ,Wtprobe=1∣At)=σtbad,π​ρtπ,\Pr_{\pi}(B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\mid A_{t})=\sigma_{t}^{\mathrm{bad},\pi}\,\rho_{t}^{\pi},

where σtbad,π:=Prπ⁡(Wtprobe=1∣Btϵ,At)\sigma_{t}^{\mathrm{bad},\pi}:=\Pr_{\pi}(W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,A_{t}) and ρtπ:=Prπ⁡(Btϵ∣At)\rho_{t}^{\pi}:=\Pr_{\pi}(B_{t}^{\epsilon}\mid A_{t}).

Proof. Fix tt. For calibration trajectory ii, let

Yi,tprobe:=𝟏​{Ai,t=1,Bi,tϵ=1,Wi,tprobe=1}Y_{i,t}^{\mathrm{probe}}:=\mathbf{1}\{A_{i,t}=1,\,B_{i,t}^{\epsilon}=1,\,W_{i,t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\}

and consider it only on active rows. On {Ai,t=1}\{A_{i,t}=1\},

𝟏​{Bi,tϵ=1,Wi,tprobe=1}\mathbf{1}\{B_{i,t}^{\epsilon}=1,\,W_{i,t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\}

is Bernoulli with parameter ptprobe,π:=Prπ⁡(Btϵ,Wtprobe=1∣At)p_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi}:=\Pr_{\pi}(B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\mid A_{t}). By Assumption 2.3, the active rows yield i.i.d. samples; Section 0.5 handles the random denominator. The Clopper–Pearson UCB gives

Pr{ptprobe,π≤ρ¯tprobe,π}≥1−δprobeT,\Pr\{p_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi}\leq\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi}\}\geq 1-\tfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}}{T},

and a union bound over t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T yields the simultaneous statement with confidence 1−δprobe1-\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}.

The factorization follows from the chain rule of conditional probability (no independence is required):

Prπ⁡(Btϵ,Wtprobe=1∣At)\displaystyle\Pr_{\pi}(B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\mid A_{t}) =Prπ⁡(Wtprobe=1∣Btϵ,At)​Prπ​(Btϵ∣At)\displaystyle=\Pr_{\pi}(W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,A_{t})\Pr_{\pi}(B_{t}^{\epsilon}\mid A_{t})
=σtbad,π​ρtπ.□\displaystyle=\sigma_{t}^{\mathrm{bad},\pi}\,\rho_{t}^{\pi}.\hskip 18.49988pt\square

If σtbad,π<1\sigma_{t}^{\mathrm{bad},\pi}<1, the probe contracts the bad-and-survive mass strictly below the bad prior; if additionally σtbad,π<σtgood,π\sigma_{t}^{\mathrm{bad},\pi}<\sigma_{t}^{\mathrm{good},\pi}, the probe also shrinks the bad-versus-good odds.

4. Proposition 2.8: Candidate-Level Evidence from EvidenceAcquire

Statement. Let Wtevid∈{0,1}W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}\in\{0,1\} denote the program-level evidence-gate survival at step tt (set to 11 when the gate is not invoked). On calibration rows that are simultaneously active, bad, and probe-surviving, let b¯tπ​(m)\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}(m) be the one-sided Clopper–Pearson UCB on

Prπ⁡(Wtevid=1∣Btϵ,Wtprobe=1,At)\Pr_{\pi}(W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,A_{t})

at level δevid/T\delta_{\mathrm{evid}}/T. Set Δ​It​(m):=−log⁡b¯tπ​(m)\Delta I_{t}(m):=-\log\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}(m). Then, with calibration probability at least 1−δevid1-\delta_{\mathrm{evid}}, simultaneously for t≤Tt\leq T,

Prπ⁡(Wtevid=1∣Btϵ,Wtprobe=1,At)≤exp⁡[−Δ​It​(m)].\Pr_{\pi}(W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,A_{t})\leq\exp[-\Delta I_{t}(m)].

Proof. Fix tt and restrict the calibration set to rows with At=1A_{t}=1, Btϵ=1B_{t}^{\epsilon}=1, and Wtprobe=1W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1. Let ntevid,πn_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi} be the number of such rows and ktevid,πk_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi} the number with Wtevid=1W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1. Conditional on this restriction, WtevidW_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}} is Bernoulli with parameter

btπ​(m):=Prπ⁡(Wtevid=1∣Btϵ,Wtprobe=1,At).b_{t}^{\pi}(m):=\Pr_{\pi}(W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,A_{t}).

By Assumption 2.3 and Section 0.5, the Clopper–Pearson UCB gives

Pr{btπ(m)≤b¯tπ(m)}≥1−δevidT,\Pr\{b_{t}^{\pi}(m)\leq\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}(m)\}\geq 1-\tfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{evid}}}{T},

and a union bound over t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T produces the good event

Gevid:={∀t≤T:btπ​(m)≤b¯tπ​(m)},Pr⁡(Gevid)≥1−δevid.G_{\mathrm{evid}}:=\{\forall t\leq T:\;b_{t}^{\pi}(m)\leq\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}(m)\},\hskip 9.24994pt\Pr(G_{\mathrm{evid}})\geq 1-\delta_{\mathrm{evid}}.

On GevidG_{\mathrm{evid}}, exp⁡[−Δ​It​(m)]=b¯tπ​(m)\exp[-\Delta I_{t}(m)]=\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}(m), so

Prπ⁡(Wtevid=1∣Btϵ,Wtprobe=1,At)=btπ​(m)≤b¯tπ​(m)=exp⁡[−Δ​It​(m)].\Pr_{\pi}(W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,A_{t})=b_{t}^{\pi}(m)\leq\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}(m)=\exp[-\Delta I_{t}(m)].

If the conditioning subset is empty, b¯tπ​(m)=1\bar{b}_{t}^{\pi}(m)=1 by Section 0.5 and the bound is trivial. □\hskip 18.49988pt\square

4.1 Suite-level interpretation

The bound treats the all-pass event over the consensus-filtered suite as a single Bernoulli channel,

Wtevid=1⇔\displaystyle W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\iff{} a bad-and-probe-surviving candidate\displaystyle\text{a bad-and-probe-surviving candidate}
passes the entire suite.\displaystyle\text{passes the entire suite}.

We calibrate the suite-level rate btπ​(m)b_{t}^{\pi}(m) directly; the mm generated tests need not be independent, and mm is not treated as a sample size.

4.2 Channel-level accumulation

If multiple evidence channels j=1,…,Jtj=1,\dots,J_{t} act on the same admission decision at step tt, with survival events Et,jE_{t,j} calibrated under sequential conditional survival

Prπ⁡(Et,j=1∣Btϵ,Wtprobe=1,At,Et,1=1,…,Et,j−1=1)≤bt,j,\Pr_{\pi}(E_{t,j}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,A_{t},\,E_{t,1}=1,\dots,E_{t,j-1}=1)\leq b_{t,j},

where each bt,jb_{t,j} is a Clopper–Pearson UCB at level δevid/(T⋅Jmax⋅|Πα|)\delta_{\mathrm{evid}}/(T\cdot J_{\max}\cdot|\Pi_{\alpha}|) on its conditional subset (with Jmax=maxt⁡JtJ_{\max}=\max_{t}J_{t}), then the chain rule gives

Prπ⁡(Wtevid=1∣Btϵ,Wtprobe=1,At)≤∏j=1Jtbt,j.\Pr_{\pi}(W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,A_{t})\leq\prod_{j=1}^{J_{t}}b_{t,j}.

In this setting we define the cumulative evidence by channel index,

ℐtevid,π:=∑j=1JtΔ​It,j,Δ​It,j:=−log⁡bt,j,\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi}:=\sum_{j=1}^{J_{t}}\Delta I_{t,j},\hskip 18.49988pt\Delta I_{t,j}:=-\log b_{t,j},

yielding

Prπ⁡(Wtevid=1∣Btϵ,Wtprobe=1,At)≤exp⁡[−ℐtevid,π].\Pr_{\pi}(W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,A_{t})\leq\exp[-\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi}].

The accumulation is over channels acting on the current step’s admission decision, not over refinement steps s≤ts\leq t. Across refinement steps, the candidates differ, no sequential conditional survival is calibrated, and the chain-rule decomposition does not apply.

For CP-Agent, the implementation uses a single TA channel per admission decision (Jt≡1J_{t}\equiv 1), and ℐtevid,π=Δ​It​(m)\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi}=\Delta I_{t}(m).

5. Validity of the Mechanism Factorization in Eq. (9)

Eq. (9) defines

q¯t,mechπ=ρ¯tprobe,π​exp⁡[−ℐtevid,π],q¯t,ctrlπ=min⁡{q¯t,rawπ,q¯t,mechπ}.\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{mech}}^{\pi}=\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi}\,\exp[-\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi}],\hskip 18.49988pt\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{ctrl}}^{\pi}=\min\{\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{raw}}^{\pi},\,\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{mech}}^{\pi}\}.

We show that on the good events of Propositions 2.7 and 2.8, q¯t,ctrlπ\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{ctrl}}^{\pi} is a valid UCB on qtπ:=Prπ⁡(Ft=1∣At)q_{t}^{\pi}:=\Pr_{\pi}(F_{t}=1\mid A_{t}).

Proof. Under the gate-semantics requirement of Section 0.2, on AtA_{t},

{Ft=1}⊆{Btϵ=1,Wtprobe=1,Wtevid=1}.\{F_{t}=1\}\subseteq\{B_{t}^{\epsilon}=1,\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\}.

The chain rule of conditional probability gives

qtπ\displaystyle q_{t}^{\pi} ≤Prπ⁡(Btϵ=1,Wtprobe=1,Wtevid=1∣At)\displaystyle\leq\Pr_{\pi}(B_{t}^{\epsilon}=1,\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\mid A_{t})
=Prπ⁡(Btϵ=1,Wtprobe=1∣At)\displaystyle=\Pr_{\pi}(B_{t}^{\epsilon}=1,\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\mid A_{t})
×Prπ⁡(Wtevid=1∣Btϵ=1,Wtprobe=1,At).\displaystyle\times\Pr_{\pi}(W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1\mid B_{t}^{\epsilon}=1,\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1,\,A_{t}).

On the good event of Proposition 2.7,

where ℐtevid,π\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi} accumulates over channels acting on the step-tt admission decision (Section 4.2). Combining,

qtπ≤ρ¯tprobe,π​exp⁡[−ℐtevid,π]=q¯t,mechπ.q_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi}\exp[-\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi}]=\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{mech}}^{\pi}.
