6. Proposition 2.9: ContextAcquire as a Calibrated Hazard Envelope

Statement. Under the split Dhistmem→Dcal→DtestD_{\mathrm{hist}}^{\mathrm{mem}}\to D_{\mathrm{cal}}\to D_{\mathrm{test}} and a frozen memory snapshot M⋆M^{\star}, ContextAcquire(k)(k) assigns h¯t+←h¯tπ​(M⋆)\underline{h}_{t+}\leftarrow\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star}), where

h¯tπ​(M⋆)=LCBBinom​(stM⋆,π,ntM⋆,π,ηh)\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star})=\mathrm{LCB}_{\mathrm{Binom}}\!\left(s_{t}^{M^{\star},\pi},\,n_{t}^{M^{\star},\pi},\,\eta_{h}\right)

is a Clopper–Pearson LCB estimated on calibration traces using M⋆M^{\star}. The increment Δ​ht​(k,Zt):=h¯tπ​(M⋆)−h¯tπ,∅\Delta h_{t}(k,Z_{t}):=\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star})-\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi,\varnothing} is the snapshot-on/off LCB gap, used only as a deployment diagnostic; the certificate uses h¯tπ​(M⋆)\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star}) directly.

Proof. Fix π\pi, tt, and M⋆M^{\star}. The split ensures that M⋆M^{\star} is constructed from DhistmemD_{\mathrm{hist}}^{\mathrm{mem}} and used read-only on DcalD_{\mathrm{cal}} and DtestD_{\mathrm{test}}, so the evaluation rows do not leak into memory construction. If M⋆M^{\star} or any other manifest entry is selected from a finite set on DcalD_{\mathrm{cal}}, all candidates are absorbed into the union bound of Theorem 2.6; the present statement is for a fixed M⋆M^{\star}.

Let ntM⋆,πn_{t}^{M^{\star},\pi} be the number of active calibration rows using M⋆M^{\star} and stM⋆,πs_{t}^{M^{\star},\pi} the count of clean successes. The deployment hazard is

htπ​(M⋆):=Prπ⁡(St=1∣At,M⋆).h_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star}):=\Pr_{\pi}(S_{t}=1\mid A_{t},\,M^{\star}).

By Assumption 2.3 and Section 0.5, on {At=1}\{A_{t}=1\} the indicator StS_{t} is i.i.d. Bernoulli with parameter htπ​(M⋆)h_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star}), and the Clopper–Pearson LCB satisfies

Pr{htπ(M⋆)≥h¯tπ(M⋆)}≥1−ηh.\Pr\{h_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star})\geq\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star})\}\geq 1-\eta_{h}.

Union-bounding over steps and any manifest-level memory/controller choices yields the simultaneous LCB. Assigning h¯t+←h¯tπ​(M⋆)\underline{h}_{t+}\leftarrow\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star}) gives ht+≥h¯tπ​(M⋆)h_{t}^{+}\geq\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M^{\star}). The certificate (Corollary 2.10, Theorem 2.6) uses this LCB directly, not the gap Δ​ht​(k,Zt)\Delta h_{t}(k,Z_{t}). □\hskip 18.49988pt\square

7. Corollary 2.10: Stopped Clean-Before-False Certificate

Statement. Fix a frozen controller π\pi. Assume the stopped-process convention of Section 0.1 and the initial-activity condition Prπ⁡(A1)=1\Pr_{\pi}(A_{1})=1. On a calibration good event giving simultaneous active-step bounds qtπ≤q¯tπq_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{q}_{t}^{\pi} and htπ≥h¯tπh_{t}^{\pi}\geq\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi} for all t≤Tt\leq T, a fresh evaluation trajectory satisfies

Prπ⁡(τS≤T,τS<τF)≥CT​(π):=[∏t=1T(1−q¯tπ)−∏t=1T(1−h¯tπ)]+.\Pr_{\pi}(\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F})\geq C_{T}(\pi):=\left[\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\bar{q}_{t}^{\pi})-\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi})\right]_{+}.

Proof. The argument uses only the chain rule on stopped events; no across-step independence is required.

Step 1 (no-false survival). The event {Ft=1}\{F_{t}=1\} implies the trajectory is active at tt, hence {Ft=1}⊆At⊆{τF>t−1}\{F_{t}=1\}\subseteq A_{t}\subseteq\{\tau_{F}>t-1\}. For events E⊆B⊆CE\subseteq B\subseteq C with Pr⁡(B)>0\Pr(B)>0,

Pr⁡(E∣C)=Pr⁡(E)Pr⁡(C)≤Pr⁡(E)Pr⁡(B)=Pr⁡(E∣B),\Pr(E\mid C)=\frac{\Pr(E)}{\Pr(C)}\leq\frac{\Pr(E)}{\Pr(B)}=\Pr(E\mid B),

so

Prπ⁡(Ft=1∣τF>t−1)≤Prπ⁡(Ft=1∣At)=qtπ≤q¯tπ.\Pr_{\pi}(F_{t}=1\mid\tau_{F}>t-1)\leq\Pr_{\pi}(F_{t}=1\mid A_{t})=q_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{q}_{t}^{\pi}.

If Pr⁡(At)=0\Pr(A_{t})=0, Section 0.4 sets the conditional to 00 and the inequality remains valid. Iterating the chain rule on {τF>t}={τF>t−1}∩{Ft=0}\{\tau_{F}>t\}=\{\tau_{F}>t-1\}\cap\{F_{t}=0\},

Prπ⁡(τF>T)=∏t=1TPrπ⁡(Ft=0∣τF>t−1)≥∏t=1T(1−q¯tπ).\Pr_{\pi}(\tau_{F}>T)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\Pr_{\pi}(F_{t}=0\mid\tau_{F}>t-1)\geq\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\bar{q}_{t}^{\pi}).

Step 2 (still-active upper bound). Since At+1=At∩{St=0,Ft=0}⊆At∩{St=0}A_{t+1}=A_{t}\cap\{S_{t}=0,\,F_{t}=0\}\subseteq A_{t}\cap\{S_{t}=0\},

Prπ⁡(At+1∣At)≤Prπ⁡(St=0∣At)=1−htπ≤1−h¯tπ.\Pr_{\pi}(A_{t+1}\mid A_{t})\leq\Pr_{\pi}(S_{t}=0\mid A_{t})=1-h_{t}^{\pi}\leq 1-\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}.

Iterating, and using Prπ⁡(A1)=1\Pr_{\pi}(A_{1})=1 from the Section 0.1 initial-activity assumption together with the inclusion AT+1⊆AT⊆⋯⊆A1A_{T+1}\subseteq A_{T}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq A_{1},

Prπ⁡(AT+1)=∏t=1TPrπ⁡(At+1∣At)≤∏t=1T(1−h¯tπ).\Pr_{\pi}(A_{T+1})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\Pr_{\pi}(A_{t+1}\mid A_{t})\leq\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}).

Step 3 (decomposition). We claim the disjoint identity

{τF>T}={τS≤T,τS<τF}∪˙AT+1.\{\tau_{F}>T\}=\{\tau_{S}\leq T,\;\tau_{S}<\tau_{F}\}\;\dot{\cup}\;A_{T+1}.

To verify it, fix a trajectory in {τF>T}\{\tau_{F}>T\} and split on whether τS≤T\tau_{S}\leq T or τS>T\tau_{S}>T:

(i) If τS≤T\tau_{S}\leq T then τS≤T<τF\tau_{S}\leq T<\tau_{F}, so the trajectory lies in {τS≤T,τS<τF}\{\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F}\}.

(ii) If τS>T\tau_{S}>T then τS>T\tau_{S}>T and τF>T\tau_{F}>T, hence the trajectory lies in AT+1={τS>T,τF>T}A_{T+1}=\{\tau_{S}>T,\,\tau_{F}>T\}.

For the reverse containment, note that the two right-hand events are disjoint: in AT+1A_{T+1} we have τS>T\tau_{S}>T, contradicting τS≤T\tau_{S}\leq T. To see that every trajectory in {τS≤T,τS<τF}\{\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F}\} also lies in {τF>T}\{\tau_{F}>T\}, we invoke the stopped-process convention of Section 0.1: on {τS<τF}\{\tau_{S}<\tau_{F}\}, τS\tau_{S} is the first stop, so Ft=0F_{t}=0 at every active step t<τSt<\tau_{S} (by minimality of τS\tau_{S}) and Ft=0F_{t}=0 at every step t>τSt>\tau_{S} (by the stopped-process zeroing); the within-step exclusivity of FτSF_{\tau_{S}} and SτSS_{\tau_{S}} via BtϵB_{t}^{\epsilon} (Section 0.1) gives FτS=0F_{\tau_{S}}=0. Hence τF=inf{t:Ft=1}=+∞>T\tau_{F}=\inf\{t:F_{t}=1\}=+\infty>T, and the trajectory is in {τF>T}\{\tau_{F}>T\}. Without this convention the identity fails (e.g., τS=2,τF=3,T=5\tau_{S}=2,\,\tau_{F}=3,\,T=5 would satisfy τS≤T,τS<τF\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F} but τF≤T\tau_{F}\leq T).

Therefore

Prπ⁡(τS≤T,τS<τF)=Prπ⁡(τF>T)−Prπ⁡(AT+1).\Pr_{\pi}(\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F})=\Pr_{\pi}(\tau_{F}>T)-\Pr_{\pi}(A_{T+1}).

Combining (14) and (15) and taking the positive part,

Prπ⁡(τS≤T,τS<τF)≥[∏t=1T(1−q¯tπ)−∏t=1T(1−h¯tπ)]+.□\Pr_{\pi}(\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F})\geq\left[\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\bar{q}_{t}^{\pi})-\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi})\right]_{+}.\hskip 18.49988pt\square

Specialization to T=1T=1. C1​(π)=[h¯1π−q¯1π]+C_{1}(\pi)=[\underline{h}_{1}^{\pi}-\bar{q}_{1}^{\pi}]_{+}, recovering the Pass@1 form.

8. Theorem 2.6: Simultaneously Valid Finite-Manifest Calibration

Statement. Let Πα\Pi_{\alpha} be a finite, pre-declared, non-empty class of frozen controllers with 1≤|Πα|<∞1\leq|\Pi_{\alpha}|<\infty, declared before DcalD_{\mathrm{cal}} is opened. Each π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha} specifies the stop/refine rule, risk-probe invocation policy, evidence intensity mm, context intensity kk, prompts, routing and deduplication rules, decoding parameters, retrievable memory snapshot M⋆M^{\star}, write mode ωwrite\omega_{\mathrm{write}}, and (when a threshold gate is used) a finite non-empty grid Θt\Theta_{t} with 1≤|Θt|<∞1\leq|\Theta_{t}|<\infty per step. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over calibration, the UCB/LCB quantities entering

CTctrl​(π):=[∏t=1T(1−q¯t,ctrlπ)−∏t=1T(1−h¯tπ​(M))]+C_{T}^{\mathrm{ctrl}}(\pi):=\left[\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{ctrl}}^{\pi})-\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1-\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M))\right]_{+}

are simultaneously valid for every π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha}, so the data-dependent selection

π⋆∈arg⁡maxπ∈Πα​CTctrl​(π)\pi^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha}}C_{T}^{\mathrm{ctrl}}(\pi)

inherits a post-selection-valid lower bound CTctrl​(π⋆)C_{T}^{\mathrm{ctrl}}(\pi^{\star}) on Prπ⋆⁡(τS≤T,τS<τF)\Pr_{\pi^{\star}}(\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F}).

8.1 Confidence budget

Choose non-negative δraw,δgate,δprobe,δevid\delta_{\mathrm{raw}},\delta_{\mathrm{gate}},\delta_{\mathrm{probe}},\delta_{\mathrm{evid}} with

δraw+δgate+δprobe+δevid≤δ.\delta_{\mathrm{raw}}+\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}+\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}+\delta_{\mathrm{evid}}\leq\delta.

For each π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha}, allocate per-row Clopper–Pearson confidences as

δraw2​T​|Πα|,δgateT​|Θt|​|Πα|,δprobeT​|Πα|,δevidT​|Πα|⋅Jmax\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{raw}}}{2T|\Pi_{\alpha}|},\hskip 9.24994pt\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}}{T|\Theta_{t}||\Pi_{\alpha}|},\hskip 9.24994pt\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}}{T|\Pi_{\alpha}|},\hskip 9.24994pt\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{evid}}}{T|\Pi_{\alpha}|\cdot J_{\max}}

for the raw, gate, probe, and evidence bounds, respectively, with Jmax=maxt⁡JtJ_{\max}=\max_{t}J_{t} (which equals 11 in the single-channel implementation). Substituting δ=0.10\delta=0.10, δ∙=0.025\delta_{\bullet}=0.025, |Πα|=5|\Pi_{\alpha}|=5, T=5T=5, |Θt|=1|\Theta_{t}|=1, Jmax=1J_{\max}=1 gives the per-row raw confidence 0.025/(2⋅5⋅5)=5×10−40.025/(2\cdot 5\cdot 5)=5\times 10^{-4} used in the main text.

8.2 Proof

For each π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha} define the good events

Graw​(π)\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{raw}}(\pi) :∀t,qtπ≤q¯t,rawπ and htπ(M)≥h¯tπ(M),\displaystyle:\forall t,\;q_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{raw}}^{\pi}\text{ and }h_{t}^{\pi}(M)\geq\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M),
Ggate​(π)\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{gate}}(\pi) :∀t,∀θ∈Θt,pt,θπ≤R¯tπ(θ),\displaystyle:\forall t,\,\forall\theta\in\Theta_{t},\;p_{t,\theta}^{\pi}\leq\bar{R}_{t}^{\pi}(\theta),
Gprobe​(π)\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{probe}}(\pi) :∀t,Prπ(Btϵ,Wtprobe=1∣At)≤ρ¯tprobe,π,\displaystyle:\forall t,\;\Pr_{\pi}(B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\mid A_{t})\leq\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi},
Gevid​(π)\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{evid}}(\pi) :∀t,∀j≤Jt,Prπ(Et,j=1∣⋯)≤bt,jπ.\displaystyle:\forall t,\,\forall j\leq J_{t},\;\Pr_{\pi}(E_{t,j}=1\mid\cdots)\leq b_{t,j}^{\pi}.

The per-row allocations of Section 8.1 give

Pr⁡(Graw​(π)c)\displaystyle\Pr(G_{\mathrm{raw}}(\pi)^{c}) ≤δraw|Πα|,\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{raw}}}{|\Pi_{\alpha}|}, Pr⁡(Ggate​(π)c)\displaystyle\Pr(G_{\mathrm{gate}}(\pi)^{c}) ≤δgate|Πα|,\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}}{|\Pi_{\alpha}|},
Pr⁡(Gprobe​(π)c)\displaystyle\Pr(G_{\mathrm{probe}}(\pi)^{c}) ≤δprobe|Πα|,\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}}{|\Pi_{\alpha}|}, Pr⁡(Gevid​(π)c)\displaystyle\Pr(G_{\mathrm{evid}}(\pi)^{c}) ≤δevid|Πα|.\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{evid}}}{|\Pi_{\alpha}|}.

Let

G:=⋂π∈Πα(Graw​(π)∩Ggate​(π)∩Gprobe​(π)∩Gevid​(π)).G:=\bigcap_{\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha}}\!\bigl(G_{\mathrm{raw}}(\pi)\cap G_{\mathrm{gate}}(\pi)\cap G_{\mathrm{probe}}(\pi)\cap G_{\mathrm{evid}}(\pi)\bigr).

A union bound over Πα\Pi_{\alpha}, steps, threshold grids, mechanism factors, and channels gives

Pr⁡(G)≥1−(δraw+δgate+δprobe+δevid)≥1−δ.\Pr(G)\geq 1-(\delta_{\mathrm{raw}}+\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}+\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}+\delta_{\mathrm{evid}})\geq 1-\delta.

On GG, for any π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha} and any t≤Tt\leq T:

  1. (1)

    qtπ≤q¯t,rawπq_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{raw}}^{\pi} from Graw​(π)G_{\mathrm{raw}}(\pi).

  2. (2)

    qtπ≤ρ¯tprobe,π​exp⁡[−ℐtevid,π]=q¯t,mechπq_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe},\pi}\exp[-\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi}]=\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{mech}}^{\pi} from Section 5 using Gprobe​(π)∩Gevid​(π)G_{\mathrm{probe}}(\pi)\cap G_{\mathrm{evid}}(\pi).

  3. (3)

    Therefore qtπ≤q¯t,ctrlπ:=min⁡{q¯t,rawπ,q¯t,mechπ}q_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{ctrl}}^{\pi}:=\min\{\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{raw}}^{\pi},\,\bar{q}_{t,\mathrm{mech}}^{\pi}\}.

  4. (4)

    htπ​(M)≥h¯tπ​(M)h_{t}^{\pi}(M)\geq\underline{h}_{t}^{\pi}(M) from Graw​(π)G_{\mathrm{raw}}(\pi).

Corollary 2.10 then gives Prπ⁡(τS≤T,τS<τF)≥CTctrl​(π)\Pr_{\pi}(\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F})\geq C_{T}^{\mathrm{ctrl}}(\pi) for every π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha}. Since GG holds simultaneously for all π∈Πα\pi\in\Pi_{\alpha}, any data-dependent π⋆\pi^{\star} in this finite class also satisfies

Prπ⋆⁡(τS≤T,τS<τF)≥CTctrl​(π⋆).\Pr_{\pi^{\star}}(\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F})\geq C_{T}^{\mathrm{ctrl}}(\pi^{\star}).

If π⋆\pi^{\star}’s manifest includes a score-threshold admission rule, Ggate​(π⋆)G_{\mathrm{gate}}(\pi^{\star}) provides the Theorem 2.5 guarantee at the corresponding threshold. □\hskip 18.49988pt\square

9. Monotonicity of the Certificate

In the unclipped regime, define

CT=∏s=1T(1−q¯s)−∏s=1T(1−h¯s),q¯t=ρ¯tprobe​exp⁡(−ℐtevid).C_{T}=\prod_{s=1}^{T}(1-\bar{q}_{s})-\prod_{s=1}^{T}(1-\underline{h}_{s}),\hskip 18.49988pt\bar{q}_{t}=\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}\exp(-\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}).

We have

∂CT∂q¯t=−∏s≠t(1−q¯s)≤0,\frac{\partial C_{T}}{\partial\bar{q}_{t}}=-\prod_{s\neq t}(1-\bar{q}_{s})\leq 0,

so any reduction in q¯t\bar{q}_{t} does not decrease CTC_{T}. Since

∂q¯t∂ρ¯tprobe=exp⁡(−ℐtevid)≥0,∂q¯t∂ℐtevid=−q¯t≤0,\frac{\partial\bar{q}_{t}}{\partial\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}}=\exp(-\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}})\geq 0,\hskip 18.49988pt\frac{\partial\bar{q}_{t}}{\partial\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}}=-\bar{q}_{t}\leq 0,

it follows that

∂CT∂ρ¯tprobe≤0,∂CT∂ℐtevid≥0,∂CT∂h¯t=∏s≠t(1−h¯s)≥0.\frac{\partial C_{T}}{\partial\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}}\leq 0,\hskip 18.49988pt\frac{\partial C_{T}}{\partial\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}}\geq 0,\hskip 18.49988pt\frac{\partial C_{T}}{\partial\underline{h}_{t}}=\prod_{s\neq t}(1-\underline{h}_{s})\geq 0.

RiskProbe contracts ρ¯tprobe\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}, EvidenceAcquire increases ℐtevid\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}, and ContextAcquire raises h¯t\underline{h}_{t}, each weakly increasing the certificate. The same conclusions hold in the clipped regime by subgradient monotonicity of [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+}.

10. Summary of Structural Conditions

  1. (1)

    Across-trajectory independence at fixed tt is required; within-trajectory step independence is not (Section 0.3).

  2. (2)

    The suite-level Bernoulli treatment does not require independence across the mm generated tests (Section 4.1); test-level independence is needed only for sequential channel accumulation (Section 4.2).

  3. (3)

    The Hypothesis Prober contributes only to ρ¯tprobe\bar{\rho}_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}; Solution Validator and Test Augmentation contribute only to ℐtevid\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}} (Sections 3, 4, 5).

  4. (4)

    Finite grids and finite manifests give post-selection validity (Theorems 2.5, 2.6).

  5. (5)

    Empty cells use the conservative conventions UCB⁡(0,0,η)=1\mathrm{UCB}(0,0,\eta)=1 and LCB⁡(0,0,η)=0\mathrm{LCB}(0,0,\eta)=0 (Section 0.5).

  6. (6)

    Memory must be frozen, or all candidate snapshots, routes, and retrieval budgets must be absorbed into Πα\Pi_{\alpha} (Section 6).

  7. (7)

    Corollary 2.10 lower-bounds Pr⁡(τS≤T,τS<τF)\Pr(\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F}), which is strictly stricter than aggregate Refine@TT or Pass@1.

  8. (8)

    FtF_{t} and StS_{t} are mutually exclusive by construction; τS=τF\tau_{S}=\tau_{F} does not occur (Section 0.1).

  9. (9)

    The mechanism containment requires Γt=1⇒Wtprobe=Wtevid=1\Gamma_{t}=1\Rightarrow W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}=1 on AtA_{t}; without it, only the raw UCB applies (Section 0.2).

  10. (10)

    The score map ϕπ\phi_{\pi}, threshold grid Θt\Theta_{t}, aggregation rule γevid\gamma_{\mathrm{evid}}, memory snapshot M⋆M^{\star}, and any calibrated scalar in rtr_{t} must be pre-declared or absorbed into Πα\Pi_{\alpha} before label counting (Section 0.6).

  11. (11)

    Evidence accumulates over channels acting on the same admission decision, not over refinement steps. The CP-Agent implementation uses a single channel per step, so ℐtevid,π=Δ​It​(m)\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{evid},\pi}=\Delta I_{t}(m) (Section 4.2).

  12. (12)

    The confidence budget satisfies δraw+δgate+δprobe+δevid≤δ\delta_{\mathrm{raw}}+\delta_{\mathrm{gate}}+\delta_{\mathrm{probe}}+\delta_{\mathrm{evid}}\leq\delta (Section 8.1).

11. Compact Proof Skeleton

  1. (1)

    Lemma (Clopper–Pearson with random active denominator). Conditioning on the active-row count, the CP UCB/LCB is valid; a union bound covers steps, grids, and manifests.

  2. (2)

    Theorem 2.5. For each (t,θ)(t,\theta), calibrate pt,θ=Pr⁡(Ft=1∣At,rt≤θ)p_{t,\theta}=\Pr(F_{t}=1\mid A_{t},\,r_{t}\leq\theta); the finite-grid simultaneous UCB yields a post-selection-valid threshold.

  3. (3)

    Proposition 2.7. On active rows, 𝟏​{Btϵ,Wtprobe=1}\mathbf{1}\{B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}}=1\} is Bernoulli; the chain rule gives the factorization σtbad​ρt\sigma_{t}^{\mathrm{bad}}\rho_{t}.

  4. (4)

    Proposition 2.8. On bad-and-probe-surviving rows, calibrate the suite-level Bernoulli survival; Δ​I=−log⁡b¯\Delta I=-\log\bar{b} requires no independence across the mm tests; channel-level accumulation requires sequential conditional calibration.

  5. (5)

    Eq. (9). The chain rule on {Ft=1}⊆{Btϵ,Wtprobe,Wtevid}\{F_{t}=1\}\subseteq\{B_{t}^{\epsilon},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{probe}},\,W_{t}^{\mathrm{evid}}\} on AtA_{t} gives qtπ≤ρ¯​exp⁡(−ℐ)q_{t}^{\pi}\leq\bar{\rho}\exp(-\mathcal{I}); the minimum with the raw UCB is again a UCB.

  6. (6)

    Proposition 2.9. With frozen M⋆M^{\star}, the active-success hazard admits the CP LCB; the snapshot-on/off gap is a diagnostic, not a certificate component.

  7. (7)

    Corollary 2.10. No-false survival lower bound, still-active upper bound, and disjoint decomposition {τF>T}={τS≤T,τS<τF}∪˙AT+1\{\tau_{F}>T\}=\{\tau_{S}\leq T,\,\tau_{S}<\tau_{F}\}\dot{\cup}A_{T+1}.

  8. (8)

    Theorem 2.6. All UCB/LCB quantities are simultaneously valid over the finite manifest; the argmax inherits the bound.

Appendix D Additional Empirical Analyses

This appendix probes the main results along seven diagnostic axes: whether Test Augmentation produces a useful signal at all (§D.1); whether Dual-Granularity Verification absorbs the TA noise we measure (§D.2); whether the gains are an artifact of weak backbones (§D.3); whether the cost–accuracy position is genuinely on the efficiency frontier (§D.4); where the tokens actually go (§D.5); how the tool budget shifts with problem difficulty (§D.6); and whether Experience’s hazard lift translates into observable per-problem savings in refinement steps and cost (§D.7). All seven analyses reuse the frozen manifest π⋆\pi^{\star} from Section 4, leaving Πα\Pi_{\alpha} and CTctrl​(π⋆)C_{T}^{\rm ctrl}(\pi^{\star}) unchanged; the detailed proofs of all theorems, propositions, and corollaries are provided in Appendix C.

D.1. Test-Augmentation Diagnostics

This analysis evaluates whether Test Augmentation (TA) provides useful candidate-level evidence beyond public tests. To avoid circular validation, the augmented tests were generated by CP-Agent with the DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat backbone, while the evaluated candidate solutions were produced independently by DeepSeek-V3.2-Reasoner on the same LCB-Pro problems.

TA label accuracy.

The diagnostic pool contains 117 problems where TA successfully generated augmented tests and the candidate solution had already passed all public tests. Among them, 5151 candidates are actually incorrect and 6666 are actually correct according to the online judge. A positive prediction means the augmented tests flag the candidate as buggy.

Although TA is an imperfect verifier, it improves the quality of the accepted set in this diagnostic pool. Before TA filtering, the hidden-bug rate is 51/117=43.6%51/117=43.6\%. Among candidates that survive TA, the hidden-bug rate drops to 11/58=19.0%11/58=19.0\%, so the post-survival correctness rate is 47/58=81.0%47/58=81.0\%.

Test-case diversity.

We estimate diversity by randomly sampling kk generated test cases from each TA suite and measuring whether at least one sampled case exposes the incorrect candidate. The evaluation is conducted on the 5151 actually-incorrect candidates from the diagnostic pool. Results are mean ±\pm standard deviation over 100100 random draws.

Detection grows steadily with kk, from 37.6%37.6\% at k=1k{=}1 to 74.5%74.5\% at k=15k{=}15. The fact that additional samples keep adding bug-detection coverage—rather than saturating after the first one or two cases—indicates that TA cases cover complementary failure modes rather than only duplicating the same signal.

D.2. Dual-Granularity Verification Robustness

This analysis targets the main failure mode exposed by the TA diagnostic: verifier-level false positives. A false positive occurs when a correct candidate fails generated augmented tests because the generated expected outputs or test conditions are noisy.

Counterfactual study.

We examine the 1919 verifier-level false-positive cases from the TA label-accuracy diagnostic. The comparison starts from the same intermediate candidate/state and runs the full CP-Agent refinement loop with TA versus without TA.

In these cases, verifier-level TA false positives do not produce observed end-to-end harm: no case succeeds without TA but fails with TA. Among the 1414 cases that remain successful in both conditions, TA introduces 5.645.64 additional steps on average to recover.

Why recovery is possible.

Dual-Granularity Verification (DGV) gives CP-Agent two independent executable feedback channels:

  • •

    Solution Validator (SV) and TA surface program-level failure signals.

  • •

    Hypothesis Prober (HP) checks local claims, brute-force comparisons, edge cases, and alternative failure hypotheses.

When these channels disagree, CP-Agent arbitrates the evidence rather than blindly trusting a single noisy verifier.

Case study: Codeforces 2098B.

In Problem 2098B, “Sasha and the Apartment Purchase”, a correct formula-based solution passes the public/basic case but fails several generated TA cases. The agent treats the signal as a possible bug and performs multiple independent HP checks:

  • •

    Step 18: first brute-force check on small instances.

  • •

    Step 19: second brute-force round with duplicates, edge cases, and re-derivation.

  • •

    Steps 20–21: stress testing and extended counterexample search.

  • •

    Step 22: additional hypotheses such as ceil-vs-floor behavior and arithmetic issues.

  • •

    Step 29: no genuine counterexample is found, so the agent retains the formula-based solution.

  • •

    Step 30: the final submission is accepted.

This illustrates the practical role of DGV: a noisy TA alarm can trigger extra validation without causing the agent to discard a correct solution.

D.3. Frontier-Backbone Transfer

This experiment applies CP-Agent to the stronger DeepSeek-V3.2-Reasoner backbone. The goal is to test whether CP-Agent only helps weaker chat backbones or remains useful when the base model already has stronger reasoning ability.

CP-Agent improves the Reasoner backbone by +9.3+9.3 Refine@5 on ICPC-Eval and +6.6+6.6 average Pass@1 on LCB-Pro. Gains concentrate on Easy and Medium problems; Hard remains unchanged, consistent with the conclusion that hard problems require stronger high-level algorithmic discovery beyond feedback utilization alone.

D.4. Efficiency and BCC Derivation

We analyze cost–performance trade-offs with Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) (Charnes et al., 1978), using the variable-returns-to-scale Banker–Charnes–Cooper (BCC) model (Banker et al., 1984). The input is average API cost per problem, and the output is Pass@1. A method is BCC-efficient when no observed method, nor any convex combination of observed methods, can achieve at least the same output with no more input. The multi-backbone Pass@1-versus-cost view supporting this analysis is shown in the main-text Figure 1.

Input-oriented BCC program.

For each decision-making unit (DMU) kk with (xk,yk)(x_{k},y_{k}), the input-oriented BCC efficiency is

minθ,{λj}\displaystyle\min_{\theta,\{\lambda_{j}\}}\quad θ\displaystyle\theta
s.t. ∑jλj​xj≤θ​xk,\displaystyle\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}x_{j}\leq\theta\,x_{k},
∑jλj​yj≥yk,\displaystyle\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}y_{j}\geq y_{k},
∑jλj=1,\displaystyle\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}=1,
λj≥0,∀j.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}\geq 0,\ \forall j.

The optimum θk⋆∈(0,1]\theta_{k}^{\star}\in(0,1]. θk⋆=1\theta_{k}^{\star}=1 means the method lies on the BCC frontier; θk⋆<1\theta_{k}^{\star}<1 means its input could be proportionally reduced by (1−θk⋆)(1-\theta_{k}^{\star}) while preserving at least the same output.

DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat data.

Let (xj,yj)(x_{j},y_{j}) denote (Cost,Pass@1)(\text{Cost},\text{Pass@1}).

AlphaCodium is Pareto-dominated by Reflexion because Reflexion has lower cost and higher Pass@1. The VRS/BCC frontier for the remaining DeepSeek points is

DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat (base)→Reflexion→CP-Agent,\text{DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat (base)}\rightarrow\text{Reflexion}\rightarrow\textsc{CP-Agent},

and these three frontier points have θ=1\theta=1.

Closed-form one-input one-output computation.

With one input, one output, and the BCC convexity constraint, any feasible reference point is a convex combination of observed DMUs. For a target output yy between two frontier outputs y1≤y≤y2y_{1}\leq y\leq y_{2}, the minimal attainable input on the frontier is obtained by linear interpolation:

λ⁡(y)\displaystyle\lambda(y) =y−y1y2−y1,\displaystyle=\frac{y-y_{1}}{y_{2}-y_{1}},
x⋆​(y)\displaystyle x^{\star}(y) =(1−λ⁡(y))​x1+λ⁡(y)​x2,\displaystyle=(1-\lambda(y))\,x_{1}+\lambda(y)\,x_{2},

D.5. Per-Component Token and Cost Breakdown

This table attributes CP-Agent’s API token usage and cost across its four main components on LCB-Pro. Results use the DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat backbone and average over 167167 problems.

HP and SV are non-LLM tools for code execution and validation; their token counts measure the associated LLM reasoning overhead, including accumulated multi-turn conversation context. TA and Experience are separate LLM calls with self-contained prompts. Costs are computed using DeepSeek API pricing.

The tracked components account for 92.4%92.4\% of total API cost. The remaining ∼7.6%\sim 7.6\% comes from problem reading, system prompts, and submission formatting. HP dominates cost because it is invoked repeatedly inside the multi-turn refinement loop, while TA and Experience together account for only 5.1%5.1\% of total cost.

D.6. Tool Use vs. Problem Difficulty

Figure 3(a) analyzes verification-tool usage along the interaction-step axis on a single backbone. This subsection complements that view with the orthogonal difficulty axis: how much tool-mediated effort CP-Agent spends per problem as problems become harder. The diagnostic uses the DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat backbone on LCB-Pro and counts the average number of HP/SV/TA invocations per problem, broken down by the benchmark’s Easy/Medium/Hard difficulty bands.

Adaptive scaling on Easy/Medium.

Compared with a fixed-pipeline baseline (each method calls every tool a constant number of times), CP-Agent issues 5.55.5 tool calls per problem on Easy and 5.15.1 on Medium. The slight drop from Easy to Medium reflects two competing effects under the certificate machinery of Section 2: (i) Medium problems trigger longer chain-of-thought before an executable candidate is produced, so HP and SV start firing later in the trajectory; (ii) once an executable candidate is produced, the admission gate Γt\Gamma_{t} continues to require evidence, so tool calls remain non-trivial. Empirically the two effects roughly cancel, and CP-Agent still relies heavily on external feedback on Easy and Medium problems.

Why Hard drops to 3.33.3.

On Hard problems, average tool calls drop to 3.33.3. This is consistent with two structural facts already documented in the main paper:

  • •

    Few executable candidates are reached. Hard problems often consume the budget on high-level algorithmic discovery before any candidate is produced. SV is only meaningful on executable candidates, and TA is only invoked when SV first returns pass on public tests; both channels stay neutral on trajectories that never reach this state. This is the same structural barrier that produces the unchanged Hard column in Table 10: refinement-loop tools cannot substitute for missing high-level ideas.

  • •

    Public-test-only filter. The augmented suite 𝒯aug\mathcal{T}_{\rm aug} is generated at most once per problem (Algorithm 1), conditional on the candidate first passing public tests. On Hard problems this trigger fires rarely, suppressing the TA contribution to the per-problem call count.

In other words, the drop on Hard is not a controller-level decision to invoke fewer tools, but a downstream consequence of the candidate stream itself becoming sparse: the gates Gi,tHP,Gi,tSV,Gi,tTAG^{\mathrm{HP}}_{i,t},G^{\mathrm{SV}}_{i,t},G^{\mathrm{TA}}_{i,t} from Algorithm 1 record neutral on inactive channels (Definition 2.1). Combined with Fig. 3(a), which shows HP concentrated in early interaction steps, this gives a coherent picture: CP-Agent spends tool budget where evidence is actionable, and remains efficient elsewhere by leaving inactive channels neutral rather than firing them spuriously.

D.7. Experience-Driven Efficiency

Section 3.3 attributes the Experience module to ContextAcquire​(k)\textsf{ContextAcquire}(k), whose effect in Proposition 2.9 is to lift the active-state success hazard h¯t​(M)\underline{h}_{t}(M). Beyond the per-step acceptance lift reported in Table 5, a higher h¯t\underline{h}_{t} should also let CP-Agent commit earlier in the refinement loop, with downstream effects on both the average number of refinement steps and the per-problem cost. We isolate this efficiency channel by an internal ablation of π⋆\pi^{\star} that toggles only the frozen Experience snapshot M⋆M^{\star} on the LCB-Pro target split (DeepSeek-V3.2-Chat backbone, manifest of Table 3).

Both axes move in the right direction.

With Experience, the average refinement step count drops and the average per-problem cost drops jointly (Fig. 6). The same direction shows up in the component ablation of Table 4: adding Experience on top of +SV+HP+TA+\textsf{SV}+\textsf{HP}+\textsf{TA} moves CP-Agent from $0.0430.043 to $0.0350.035 per problem and improves the only-solved #​T\#T on ICPC-Eval from 2.22.2 to 1.81.8, while raising LCB-Pro Pass@1 from 46.146.1 to 48.548.5. Two measurement axes—LCB-Pro all-problem average in Fig. 6 and ICPC-Eval only-solved #​T\#T in Table 4—thus agree on the sign of the effect, while differing in absolute magnitude due to the averaging convention.

Mechanism interpretation.

The cost reduction is not driven by Experience being a cheaper module: Table 13 shows Experience itself consumes only ∼3.4%\sim\!3.4\% of the total tracked API cost. Instead, the savings act through the certificate state. A higher h¯t​(M)\underline{h}_{t}(M) lets the admission gate Γt\Gamma_{t} close earlier on the trajectories that would otherwise have continued, which in turn truncates the HP/SV invocations downstream of those refinement steps. Since HP and SV together account for 87.3%87.3\% of tracked cost (Table 13), the saved HP/SV calls dominate the additional retrieval cost incurred by Experience. In the language of Section 2, ContextAcquire converts hazard lift into refinement-step savings, and the savings on the expensive verification channels outweigh the retrieval overhead—giving the qualitative claim in Section 4 that “retrieved repair experiences reduce ineffective trial-and-error” a concrete per-problem efficiency signature.

Appendix E Datasets

ICPC-Eval (Xu et al., 2026)

is a competitive-programming benchmark designed to reflect real contest settings. It is built from problems drawn from 1111 recent ICPC contests (collected via QOJ and VJudge): starting from 139139 problems, the dataset is cleaned and finalized to 118118 problems. It filters out problems that rely on crucial non-textual figures, interactive problems, or problems without an official reference solution. For tasks requiring special judging, ICPC-Eval retains them and additionally implements 1212 custom special judges (e.g., for floating-point outputs or multiple valid answers). All problem statements are standardized into LaTeX for consistent parsing and model input. The benchmark matches ICPC-style problem diversity and difficulty, and provides annotations over eight major algorithmic areas (e.g., DP, mathematics, graph algorithms, and data structures), with many problems spanning multiple areas to capture the compositional and challenging nature of ICPC problems.

LiveCodeBench Pro (Zheng et al., 2026)

is a challenging benchmark for evaluating large language models on competitive programming. Its central goal is to mitigate overestimation caused by training-data contamination by maintaining a continuously updated problem set. The benchmark curates problems from top-tier contests such as Codeforces, ICPC, and IOI. Problems are collected as soon as possible after they appear in real contests, further reducing the risk of data leakage.

Appendix F Metrics

Refine@K (Xu et al., 2026)

is an execution-feedback-based evaluation metric designed to measure an LLM’s ability to iteratively improve a solution under a bounded turn budget. In ICPC-Eval, each problem is solved through up to KK response–refinement chances, and the metric asks whether the model can “pass the test within response and refinement chances” (i.e., succeed within KK turns). Concretely, the evaluation is multi-turn: in the first turn, the model receives the full problem statement; in subsequent turns, the model is additionally provided with its previous response and the corresponding evaluation feedback. Thus, a model is counted as successful under Refine@K if any of its first KK attempts (conditioned on prior code + feedback) produces a correct program. Compared with Pass@K (independent resampling), Refine@K better captures the behavior of reasoning/reflection-capable models because it explicitly evaluates whether a model can use feedback to correct mistakes rather than merely getting lucky with another sample.

# Turn (Xu et al., 2026)

represents the average number of correct response turns, computed only over problems that are successfully solved within the refinement budget. Specifically, for each solved problem, we record the turn index at which the model first produces a correct solution, and then average this index across the solved subset. A smaller #T indicates the model typically fixes its solution within fewer turns, suggesting more efficient use of execution feedback, whereas a larger #T implies the model often needs more trial-and-error refinement rounds before arriving at a correct program.

Pass@1

measures the single-try success rate of code generation: for each problem, the model produces exactly one candidate solution (one response/submission). If this first solution passes the evaluation (e.g., all test cases), the problem is counted as solved. Pass@1 is the fraction of problems solved on the first attempt:

Pass@1=1N∑i=1N𝕀[\displaystyle\mathrm{Pass@1}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}\big[ the model’s first solution for
problem i passes].\displaystyle\text{problem }i\text{ passes}\big].

Intuitively, Pass@1 reflects the model’s initial answer quality without any retries or feedback-driven refinement, in contrast to iterative metrics such as Refine@K.

## Analysis Requirements

### 1. Identify the Root Cause - What is the fundamental cause of this error? - Is it an algorithmic logic issue, a boundary-condition issue, or a syntax/library-usage issue?

### 2. Extract the Fix Strategy - What specific method did the agent use to fix the issue? - What are the key steps of this fix? - Are there any debugging tricks or thought processes worth recording?

### 3. Summarize Reusable Experience - If a similar issue occurs in the future, what approach should be taken? - What was the most critical insight in this fix process? - What general cautions or best practices apply?

## Output Format Requirements

Return a JSON object with the following fields: 

{
  "error\_context": "When/where the error occurred (what was being implemented/handled)",
  "error\_cause": "The specific cause of the error",
  "fix\_method": "The concrete modification made",
  "fix\_result": "The effect after the fix",
  "key\_insight": "A reusable key takeaway (one-sentence lesson)"
}

### Output Specifications

1. error_context (required): - Describe the scenario and timing of the error. - Examples: "While implementing divide-and-conquer optimized DP", "When handling large-scale array inputs", "When enumerating subsets using bit operations". - Length: 10--30 words.

2. error_cause (required): - Clearly state the cause of the error. - Examples: "Incorrect subproblem evaluation order in recursion, violating state dependencies." - Examples: "Using <= in the loop bound caused out-of-bounds array access." - Length: 15--50 words.

3. fix_method (required): - Describe the concrete fix. - Examples: "Move the recursive call solve(l, mid-1) before computing dp[mid]." - Examples: "Change the loop condition from i<=n to i<n." - Length: 15--50 words.

4. fix_result (required): - Describe the effect after applying the fix. - Examples: "State dependencies are satisfied; outputs match expected results." - Examples: "All array accesses are within bounds; no segmentation fault." - Length: 10--30 words.

5. key_insight (required): - The most important reusable lesson. - It should help others avoid the same mistake at a glance. - Examples: "In divide-and-conquer DP optimization, subproblems that the current state depends on must be computed before evaluating dp[mid]." - Examples: "Array indices range from 0 to n-1; use a strict < n loop bound when iterating." - Length: 20--60 words.

Appendix H Case Study

Given the substantial length of both the inputs and outputs of CP-Agent, we limit the presentation below to the full problem description, CP-Agent’s tool-use behavior, and the final submission.

Problem

Alea Iacta Est

https://qoj.ac/contest/1662/problem/8684

Time limit: 10000 ms
Memory limit: 1024 MB

Description

You play a game with multiple fair six-sided dice. Each die’s face displays a single symbol. The objective of the game is to roll the dice and create a valid word from the symbols on top of each die. If you cannot form a word, you may reroll the dice for another attempt.

Suppose there are five dice: one of them contains letters A, B, C, D, E, and P (abbreviated as ABCDEP), and the other dice contain AEHOXU, AISOLR, ABCDEF, and ABCSCC. The first roll yields the following letters on the tops of respective dice: P,X,R,EP,X,R,E, and SS. As it is impossible to arrange these letters into a valid word, you decide to keep the P,SP,S, and EE, and reroll the other dice, in an attempt to make words like PARSE, PAUSE, PHASE, POISE, PROSE, PULSE, or PURSE. The two dice yield EE and AA, resulting in the following five letters: P,E,A,EP,E,A,E, and SS. You still cannot think of a valid word, so you decide to keep four letters and reroll only the last die, which has three sides with letter C. By doing so, there is a 50%50\% chance that it will be possible to make a final valid word: PEACE, as shown in Figure K.1.

When you roll a die, it lands on any one of its faces with equal probability. What is the expected number of rolls needed to make a valid word, assuming you use an optimal strategy?

Input

The first line of input contains two numbers dd and ww, where d⁡(1≤d≤6)d\ (1\leq d\leq 6) is the number of dice and w⁡(1≤w≤2⋅105)w\ (1\leq w\leq 2\cdot 10^{5}) is the number of valid words in the dictionary. The following dd lines each have 66 symbols, one for each face of the die. The final ww lines contain ww distinct valid words in the dictionary. Every word has exactly dd symbols.

All symbols in the input are either uppercase letters (A--Z) or digits (0--9).

Output

If it is possible to make a valid word, output the expected number of rolls needed to make a valid word when using an optimal strategy. Otherwise, output impossible. Your answer should have an absolute or relative error of at most 10−610^{-6}.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

const double INF = 1e18;
const double EPS = 1e-12;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int d, w;
    cin >> d >> w;

    vector<string> dice(d);
    for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) {
        cin >> dice[i];
        // each dice[i] has exactly 6 characters
    }

    vector<string> words(w);
    for (int i = 0; i < w; i++) {
        cin >> words[i];
    }

    // Preprocess words: sort characters
    unordered_set<string> wordSet;
    for (string& wrd : words) {
        string sorted = wrd;
        sort(sorted.begin(), sorted.end());
        wordSet.insert(sorted);
    }

    int total_configs = pow(6, d);

    // faces[config][i] = face index of die i
    vector<vector<int>> faces(total_configs, vector<int>(d));
    vector<bool> win(total_configs, false);
    bool any_win = false;

    for (int id = 0; id < total_configs; id++) {
        int tmp = id;
        vector<char> symbols(d);
        for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) {
            int f = tmp % 6;
            tmp /= 6;
            faces[id][i] = f;
            symbols[i] = dice[i][f];
        }
        string sorted_sym(symbols.begin(), symbols.end());
        sort(sorted_sym.begin(), sorted_sym.end());
        if (wordSet.count(sorted_sym)) {
            win[id] = true;
            any_win = true;
        }
    }

    if (!any_win) {
        cout << "impossible" << endl;
        return 0;
    }

    // DP arrays
    vector<double> dp(total_configs, 0.0);
    vector<double> dp_new(total_configs, 0.0);
    for (int i = 0; i < total_configs; i++) {
        dp[i] = win[i] ? 0.0 : 1000.0; // initial guess
    }

    // Precompute popcount and powers of 6
    vector<int> popcount(1 << d, 0);
    for (int m = 0; m < (1 << d); m++) {
        popcount[m] = __builtin_popcount(m);
    }
    vector<double> pow6(d + 1, 1.0);
    for (int i = 1; i <= d; i++) {
        pow6[i] = pow6[i - 1] * 6.0;
    }

    // Precompute offsets for sum array
    int total_partial = pow(7, d);
    vector<double> sum(total_partial, 0.0);

    vector<int> offset(1 << d, 0);
    int cur_offset = 0;
    for (int m = 0; m < (1 << d); m++) {
        offset[m] = cur_offset;
        cur_offset += pow(6, popcount[m]);
    }
    


    // Helper: compute projection id for config id and mask
    auto getProjId = [&](int config_id, int mask) -> int {
        int proj_id = 0;
        int base = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) {
            if (mask >> i & 1) {
                int face = faces[config_id][i];
                proj_id += face * base;
                base *= 6;
            }
        }
        return proj_id;
    };

    // Value iteration
    int iter = 0;
    double max_diff;
    do {
        // Update sum array
        fill(sum.begin(), sum.end(), 0.0);
        for (int c = 0; c < total_configs; c++) {
            double val = dp[c];
            for (int m = 0; m < (1 << d); m++) {
                int proj_id = getProjId(c, m);
                int idx = offset[m] + proj_id;
                sum[idx] += val;
            }
        }

        // Compute dp_new
        max_diff = 0.0;
        for (int c = 0; c < total_configs; c++) {
            if (win[c]) {
                dp_new[c] = 0.0;
                continue;
            }
            double best = INF;
            int full_mask = (1 << d) - 1;
            for (int R = 0; R < full_mask; R++) {
                int U = full_mask ^ R;
                int k = popcount[U];
                int proj_id = getProjId(c, R);
                int idx = offset[R] + proj_id;
                double expected = 1.0 + sum[idx] / pow6[k];
                if (expected < best) best = expected;
            }
            dp_new[c] = best;
            max_diff = max(max_diff, fabs(dp_new[c] - dp[c]));
        }

        swap(dp, dp_new);
        iter++;
    } while (max_diff > EPS && iter < 5000);

    // Compute initial expected rolls
    double total = 0.0;
    for (int c = 0; c < total_configs; c++) {
        total += dp[c];
    }
    double ans = 1.0 + total / pow6[d];

    cout << fixed << setprecision(9) << ans << endl;
    return 0;
}

Appendix I Extended Discussion on Related Work

LLM Agents.

Large Language Models have been increasingly deployed as autonomous agents capable of interacting with external environments and solving multi-step tasks. In the domain of web navigation, researchers have developed agents to autonomously browse and interact with online interfaces (Ning et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Lai et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). In the field of software engineering, agents such as SWE-Agent have been proposed to handle repository-level maintenance and development tasks (Luo et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025). Furthermore, the application of agents has extended to high-level intellectual domains, including automated scientific discovery (Toledo et al., 2026; Baek et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2024) and data science analysis, where agents assist in data visualization and interpretation (Zhu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024). These advancements collectively demonstrate the potential of LLM agents to generalize across diverse and complex workflows.

In contrast to the extensive body of work on autonomous agents interacting with dynamic external environments, a more focused stream of research investigates Agentic Reasoning—the use of deterministic tools to enhance the model’s internal cognitive processes. Unlike autonomous agents that use tools as “effectors” to change the environment state, this paradigm employs tools—primarily code interpreters (e.g., Python) and calculators—as “cognitive prosthetics” to ground the reasoning process itself. Early works such as PAL (Gao et al., 2023) and PoT (Chen et al., 2022b) demonstrated that decoupling reasoning from computation significantly reduces hallucinations in mathematical and symbolic tasks. Advancing this trajectory, recent frameworks (Wu et al., 2025; Gou et al., 2024; Das et al., 2024; Shang et al., 2025) establish a more sophisticated interleaved reasoning–action loop. By integrating code execution directly into the chain of thought, these methods utilize deterministic feedback for iterative step verification and error correction, enabling the model to navigate complex logical paths with higher reliability. Although fewer in number compared to general agent papers, these studies highlight a critical distinction: for challenging reasoning tasks, the value of a tool lies not in its complexity or connectivity, but in its ability to provide deterministic, verifiable feedback that constrains the model’s probabilistic output.

Competitive Programming.

Program synthesis has evolved significantly from early deductive (Manna and Waldinger, 1980) and inductive (Spector and Robinson, 2002) synthesis to neural approaches like DeepCoder (Balog et al., 2016). However, the release of challenging benchmarks (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Jain et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026) revealed a harsh reality: early models failed near-completely on competition-level problems. AlphaCode (Li et al., 2022) marked a major milestone in this domain by leveraging massive sampling for competitive programming problems, while AlphaCode2 (Leblond et al., 2023) and OpenAI’s o1-ioi (El-Kishky et al., 2025) later adopted reinforcement learning and heuristic inference strategies to achieve gold-medal performance. Most recently, OpenAI o3 (OpenAI, 2025a) demonstrated that general-purpose reasoning models could reach Grandmaster status on Codeforces without domain-specific hand-crafting.

Since training such reasoning models is computationally prohibitive, recent research has pivoted to inference-time enhancements using hand-crafting LLM workflows like MapCoder (Islam et al., 2024), AlphaCodium (Ridnik et al., 2024), and CODESIM (Islam et al., 2025). These methods simulate human problem-solving through iterative “generate-and-verify” cycles. However, they mainly rely on fixed, stateless workflows, which suffer from rigidity: they lack the adaptivity to scale reasoning effort within a problem, and crucially, they fail to transfer experience across problems, discarding valuable debugging insights after each session. This limitation highlights the need for more dynamic and long-term evolving mechanisms.
